en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Huanglong Huītáng Xīn by Xú Xí of Xī'ān.
In the second year of the Xīníng era, the National Teacher Nán of Mount Huánglóng in Hóngzhōu entered into meditative repose. The Prefecture appointed his disciple, Master Xīn, [to succeed him].

He succeeded to the position and ascended the seat at Yunyan Monastery in the county. I invited some ten of my fellow students to burn incense and stand by his side to listen to what he called his "Instructions to the Assembly.
Prior to this, I had already known of the Master; upon reaching this point, my conviction was further strengthened and I marveled at him.
Consequently, I resolved to study under him for four years. We took up residence in the western room of the hall, and more than two [months] passed.
From early morning until dusk, he devoted himself to his studies according to that method. For over six years, he traveled through the capital and subsequently through the mountains.

The following year, having received leave, he went home and hosted the Master at the Yan-yuan (Cave Temple) below Hanxi. From that first meeting until this present time, he has personally received [the Master’s] instruction.
Yet those who hear it in great detail soon forget it upon turning their heels, unable to retain it in memory. Another year passed, and I became a Censor.
His disciple, Huizhe, then compiled and recorded what he had heard and requested that I write a preface for it. I replied to him, saying:
Who is it that speaks of the Way? Yet your master has falsely spoken of it. Who is it that speaks these words? Yet you, my followers, have falsely listened to them.
Who is it that speaks and who is it that listens? And yet you invite me to falsely compose a preface for them.

Although so be it—since your master has already constantly spoken falsely, and you, my followers, have likewise constantly listened falsely—why alone should I not falsely compose a preface for you? If...
If even this is considered delusory, then where could one go without knowing what is delusory?
Where could one go without acting delusorily? Only by [recognizing this] might one perhaps avoid being delusory.
The Recorded Sayings of Venerable Master Huanglong Huítáng Xīn,
compiled by Attendant Zhīhé and re-edited by Disciple Zhòngjiè.
The Master ascended the hall. At that time, while he was before the Dharma seat and the great assembly had gathered and settled, he smiled after a long silence and said:
"To let it rest just like this would already be a deception. Do you understand this thoroughly? If you do, you may well take advantage of this moment;
if not, do not mistakenly try to grasp the moon in the water. He then ascended the seat and burned incense, offering it for...

May the present Emperor prolong his sacred life; may the Dragon Chart be eternally firm and the Phoenix Calendar ever renewed. May the realm be peaceful and secure, and may the Wheel of Dharma turn perpetually.
The Master then sat in the full lotus posture. Holding up his whisk, he said: "If you call this a whisk, the entire school of Bodhidharma will be swept away and utterly extinguished.
If you do not call it a whisk, waves arise upon level ground. Arriving at this point, it is like a long sword leaning against the heavens—dare anyone face its edge?
To hesitate for a moment is to lose one's life. Is there anyone here now who can strike it and shatter it?"
Han. To test and determine [the truth], observe: At that time, there was a monk who came forth from the assembly and prostrated. The Master said, "I do not know whether you are right or wrong.
The monk said, "Nor should you let this pass. The Master said, "Do not disbelieve the Way. He asked, "The Way is fundamentally without words; it is through words that the Way is revealed.
As a student who has come here, I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "When walking reaches the end of the water, sit and watch."
When the clouds arose, a monk asked, "Is this not the very point of acting for others? The Master said, "But you are not alert.
The monk said, "If one does not climb the tower to look out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean? The Master said, "What is the matter of that depth?
The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout! The monk said, "I almost let it pass. The Master said, "As for a patch-robed monk such as this..."
Kanchi Lun asked, "What is the realm of Yuzhang? The Master said, "The waves are vast upon Longsha; the peaks are high at Heling.
The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Holding a dragon-tusked staff in hand, he idly seeks the moon-calling monkeys.
The monk asked, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the person and the realm; as for the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, what is it like? The Master said, "Not."
"This is one who knows; it is merely a laborious talk about the cold of winter. The monk said, "If that is so, then the Way is prosperous and the Son of Heaven’s edict is not transmitted;
the times are clear and all sing songs of great peace. The Master said, "Excessive ritual leads to chaos. The monk asked, "How was it before you ascended this seat?
The Master said, "There was nothing at all. The monk asked, "How is it after ascending? The Master said, "Looking up with one's face."
The Master said, "Heaven does not see heaven. The monk said, "In that case, all stars bow toward the North, and no water does not flow toward the East.
The Master said, "Idle talk.
He added, "In general, when investigating the root source of birth and death, you must directly realize your own plot of land."
Instruct them clearly regarding where they should go, so that they may apply this according to the situation as it arises without missing the proper occasion.

It is just like before the slightest sign of a blade’s edge has emerged—there is neither "this" nor "that"—yet in an instant, when it suddenly flares up, there are already the five elements of metal and earth.
Mutually generating and mutually overcoming; when the barbarian comes, the Han appears. The four castes dwell together, each occupying their own region.

Right and wrong arise like sharp blades, causing black and yellow to be indistinguishable and water and milk to remain unmixed. The ailment has reached the vital organs and the diaphragm, making it difficult to treat.

If this is not clearly revealed in the presence of the sun, the impoverished son will have no way to know his home. If you wish for the Great Function to manifest before you, you need only suddenly forget.
All views. Once all views are exhausted, the dark mist does not arise; great wisdom is luminously clear, no longer being anything else.
Be careful. On the first day of the month, he ascended the hall. "The moon gives birth to one. Cold has come; white light arises in the empty chamber. "The moon gives birth to two.

The peach blossoms have already revealed the intent of Lingyun. "The moon gives birth to three. Samantabhadra remains unmoving while Mañjuśrī makes his inquiry. He then raised his whisk and said: "Exhausted!"
"Entering this gate of samādhi—do you see it? The green mountains cannot conceal it; the bright moon, however, allows it to be contained.
With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "To know illusion is to be detached from it; no expedient means are required. To be detached from illusion is to awaken; there is likewise no gradual process.

Śākyamuni the Old One has, in a single stroke, flung open a thousand gates and ten thousand doors. A man of keen intelligence, upon hearing this mentioned, seizes his staff and goes forth immediately.
If you hesitate further, you will find yourself heading for Xiqin while I am off to Donglu."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes I open the gate to wait for a worthy guest, yet the worthy guest does not come to pass by.

Sometimes I take their hand and climb the high mountain, yet those on the high mountain do not look back. At times I act as a defeated general, joining my hands in surrender before the hands of the *śrāmaṇera*.
At other times I become the wrathful Nanda, striking the bone and breaking the marrow. When it is exactly like this, is there anyone who agrees?"
"Like sounds responding to one another; like kind spirits seeking each other out. If you have it, then take a step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole.
If you do not, then before the peak of Shaoshi, you are but a source of laughter.
Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation bench once and said: "When a single speck of dust is raised, the entire earth is fully contained within it.
The ears of all of you are within this one sound; this one sound pervades the ears of all of you. If you are a soaring falcon that cleaves the clouds, you ought to seize the moment."
"To try to keep fish in a stagnant pond is merely to labor in vain by churning up the waves.
He ascended the hall and said: "Dharma came for nine years at Shaoshi; he deserves thirty lashes. Yet he comes here to deceive the descendants of this land.
Old Lu left Huangmei in the middle of the night; how laughable that he claims it was not sharp-witted. I transmitted it at the third watch."
Regarding the Dharma for receiving robes: Today, Yellow Dragon, while walking, did not hesitate to swing his arms about;
he intended to flash forth one eye, yet he wished to add frost to snow. He then raised his whisk and said: "Do you see the Patriarch?"
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "How was it before the Prince ascended the throne? The Master said, "Entering a village, one follows its customs. The monk asked, "And after he had ascended?
The Master said, "The four seas and five lakes are all within the realm of his royal transformation. The monk asked, "I wonder, is there still something beyond this?
The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is that which is beyond? The Master said, "Putting on one's robes."
"What difficulty is there in eating a meal?
He spoke again: "If I were to let out a single thread of a path, you might follow it by asking about the east and answering about the west.
But if I do not let out a single thread of a path, where else will you go to grope for it? It is better to return to the banks of the Xiang River."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year: The old year has already departed; the new year follows in succession. One departs and one arrives, never for a moment interrupted.
Thus we know that the Great Mass of Being is in constant flux; every thing is impermanent. Within a single *kṣaṇa*, there is the new and the old.
That which is new can manifest as brilliance and beauty, as filaments and fragrance; it may pour forth or blow, it may soar or leap.
That which is ancient can become dust, a parasite, dull, or obscured; it may be loathed or abandoned, cut away or destroyed.
Such birth and death, such transformation and passage, cannot be observed through physical forms or instruments, nor can they be grasped through feelings or falsehoods.
One must trace its roots and its source: when it comes, one does not know whence it comes; when it goes, one does not know whither it goes.
For those who recognize this, it is immediately the functioning of the divine; for those who do not know, another year is added to the new year.
Take care. Ascending the hall: To go is not to go; to stay is not to stay. Birth and death, nirvana—there is originally nothing to avoid or fear therein.
Whether noble or base, one simply observes the buying and selling; never departing from the marketplace, ten thousand waves arise in competition—all are Mañjuśrī.
The family style is a single expanse of clear sky; there is nothing that is not the realm of Samantabhadra. If you depart from words and letters, it is like mistaking a thief for your son;
if you cling to words and letters, you are instead mistaking your son for a thief. Having been informed thus, do you recognize a sense of shame? Or not?
Ascending the hall, he said: "To not consort with the myriad dharmas is the Samādhi of Non-contention. If you proceed in this manner, what can be done?
For when the string is taut, the sound is short. If you can scatter genuine pearls within the purple silk curtain, it will not necessarily be that a virtuous cause invites an evil result."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The Patriarch said, 'To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-view; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-realization.
These are excellent words! One must urgently achieve resonance with them. It is not apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, yet it is not identical to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
To fully realize that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty—how could such a person differ from the Buddha? Do you understand? As I am about to rise, I cannot carry [the answer] away."
Departing, at one moment they intersect with the spring breeze.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "I possess true gold that has been refined a hundred times; skillfulness and clumsiness are both transformations produced by human hands.
Worldly names are merely provisional appellations, following along like jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets. O practitioners of Zen, the myriad phenomena of the universe do not obstruct the eye."
Guang. For what reason did he say, "Whether one sees or does not see, it is simply because clarity is ultimate that what is attained is delayed"?

He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "At the place where words cannot reach, I request the Master to grant us instruction. The Master said, "When the clouds have vanished, the sun and moon are just right."
"The snow has cleared; heaven and earth are spring. A monk asked, "What is it like when one goes forth in this very manner? The Master said, "Where would you fall?
The monk lifted the corner of his *kāṣāya*. The Master said, "I let you off with one stroke."
He spoke again: "The fishing line hangs a thousand feet, yet its intent lies in the deep pool. He then raised his whisk and said: "Behold!
The life-long pursuit of the scarlet-tailed, brocade-scaled fish—do not cast your line haphazardly."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not.
To simply rest thus would be to pull up the oars, secure the lines, and moor the boat within the bay.
But according to the school of the patch-robed monks, this is worlds apart. Tell me, what excellence does the school of the patch-robed monks possess? The staff lies across."
Carrying his burden, he disregards all others and goes straight into the thousands and tens of thousands of peaks.
He ascends the hall. A monk asks: "Dragons and elephants have all gathered at the side of the seat; as guest and host interact with one another, what is your intention? The Master says:
"Look for yourself," the Master said. The monk replied, "With his body spanning the universe, there is still one who emerges from it.

The Master asked, "How can you ask such a question without having eyes? The monk said, "If one does not enter the tiger's den, how can one see the tiger's cubs? The Master said, "Even if you leap over the Dragon Gate, the wind and waves will be even more perilous."
He spoke again: "If you always take the principle from within words, you are like a water jellyfish that uses a shrimp for eyes.
What would you do if you were suddenly to cut off the essential pass? How would you then find a way to settle there? He struck the meditation seat once and said, "Pass!"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. When the ancients spoke thus, it was like peering at a leopard through a tube;
one sees but a single spot. Even if one enters the forest without stirring the grass and enters the water without disturbing the waves, this is still like riding a horse across jagged ice.
If you have the hand of an eagle-slayer, why not rub it upon the head of a snake?
Itch! Those who have passed through the barrier, try to discern this.
Entering the hall: When the autumn light is clear and shallow, the white dew mingles with the misty isles.
How excellent is Avalokiteśvara, his entire body entering the wild grasses! Clearly proclaimed, clearly revealed. After thirty years, do not fail those who are well-intentioned.

Ascending the hall, he said: "One does not point toward; two does not open up. Turning my thoughts back, I consider Nanyue and Tiantai—how laughable that the white clouds have no fixed abode, blown away by the wind and then blown back again."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall? The Master said, "I am poor and have no blanket to cover me.
The monk asked, "Are you not being ungrateful toward the former sages? The Master said, "And what is your own understanding, Reverend?
The monk drew a circle. The Master said, "The swallow does not leave its nest. The monk bowed. The Master said, "It is getting late."
"It is still tolerable; it is only after midday that one begins to feel the sorrow. A monk asked, "When Minister Pei visited Huangbo and Li Ao ascended Yaoshao, what was the underlying meaning?
The Master said, "The moonlight is seen in stillness; the sound of the spring is heard in the depths.
The monk said, "Auspicious clouds reach everywhere. The Master said, "Those with eyes will discern this."

He spoke again: "As long as one has not realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of discrimination arise. Once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises, and one then abandons the appearances of external dust.
O virtuous practitioners of dhyāna, consider for a moment the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as light and darkness, form and emptiness."
Dharma after Dharma manifests before one. How can you explain the principle of relinquishment? Do you understand it clearly yet?
If you listen with your ears, you will never comprehend it; only when hearing sound through the faculty of the eye will you know it.

Entering the Prefecture and Returning to the Hall: When I left, the spring wind was high, sweeping away the snow from a thousand mountains. When I return, the spring grasses are deep; the cuckoo cries all the more piteously. How marvelous!
The Dharma-gate of Universal Sustenance (Dhāraṇī) is everywhere. In my sorrow, I speak for your sake, for there is no other cause.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. A man of clear eyes cannot be deceived for even a single point.
You who say 'it is the mind of the benevolent one that moves'—wait a moment! Where do you see the Patriarch? He then struck the ground with his whisk and said:
"Look. He ascended the hall and said, "The true Dharma-body of the Buddha is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.

How do you explain this principle of 'responding'? He then raised his whisk and asked, "Do you see it? Fortunately, there is no place where its light does not shine. Just as he spoke, [a monk] stepped forward. The Master struck him with the whisk and said, "A stiff fellow!"

On a day when it was not yet clear, he ascended the hall and said: "Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure hidden upon the tip of Huanglong’s whisk.
If I were to offer it for sale to you all, neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how would you appraise it? He remained silent.
The person overpaid; he struck him and gave him three hundred.
On the anniversary of the former master’s passing, he ascended the hall: "Last year, on the seventeenth day of the third month, a night wind shook the counting-chip chamber."
The three-legged qilin has entered the heart of the sea; only a sliver of the moon remains, emerging from the waves. Truth does not conceal falsehood, nor does curvature hide the straight.
Who will join me in this song of snow? Those who share this understanding through all eternity are those of today.
Ascending the hall, he cited the teaching that all sentient beings—these various manifestations of illusion—are born from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment.
The Master said: "The Buddhas of the three periods are illusions; the entire Great Canon is an illusion; Bodhidharma’s coming from the West is an illusion;
and as for the old monks throughout the land, even extending to the entirety of heaven and earth, the sun, moon, and stars—all are nothing but illusions."
"This is an illusion. What, then, is the wondrous mind? After a long silence, he said: "Let the embroidered mandarin ducks be viewed as they are;
do not pass the golden needle to others."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Where there is obstruction, it is not a wall; where there is penetration, it is not empty space. If you can understand it in this way, mind and form are fundamentally the same.
This whisk is form; which one is mind? O clever ones! As soon as you hear it mentioned, you see the horn through the wall and already know it is an ox.
If you hesitate or deliberate further, white clouds will stretch for thousands and tens of thousands of miles."
Ascending the hall, he said: "This very mind, mind, mind is Buddha—the most wondrous sentient being in the worlds of the ten directions.
Its transverse and vertical marvelous functions are truly pitiable; nothing else compares to the reality of this mind. You people, do not vainly seek Bodhi;
Bodhi cannot be seen. Do not vainly eliminate afflictions; afflictions have no front or back. Before any signs have arisen, it is the original state."
There is no change. If one speaks of "meeting" or "not meeting," all are merely three heads and two faces.
To ask further "how" or "what"—alas for the Buddha!
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddhas of the past have already passed away; the Buddhas of the future have not yet been born.
Right now, in the present, the Buddha-dharma is entrusted to Huanglong. If you let it go, it is hazy and indistinct, yet within it there is substance.
If you hold it fast, it is profound and obscure, yet within it there is essence. Tell me: is it letting go? Or is it holding fast? It is like the thread on the tip of a fishing pole."
"Playing with you from the start; not violating the clear waves, my intent is naturally distinct.
[He] ascends the hall: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree. Let everyone nod their heads as they please.
But when the tree falls and the vine withers, there is no scheme to pierce the heavens above, nor any plot to enter the earth below. O sharp-witted ones, apply yourselves here!"
Having gained one eye, one immediately sees in all directions, moving freely and unhindered. He then raised his whisk and said: "Look! The great sun overflows the eyes;
ten thousand miles away, not a single speck of cloud hangs in the sky. But for those beneath a covered basin, how can they blame the mountain monk?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If we discuss this matter, the Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) never actually crossed the river, and the Second Patriarch never truly obtained the marrow.

Yet, when it came to the midnight at Huangmei, one person spread a falsehood and ten thousand people spread it as truth. According to Old Lu’s (Huineng’s) own insight, he was merely a man of the rice-pounding shed.
To this day, people have traveled all over the world, yet they do not realize that this very plot of land has been entrusted [to them]."
It has also been a long time since they arrived. Because these people were unwilling to take up the succession, thorns and brambles have gradually grown while the grain has failed to sprout.
They run hither and thither, seeking but a few pints of food each day. How much better it would be to simply recognize, right here and now, the original deed of ownership;
to make its four boundaries and limits clearly distinct, so that one may avoid seeing things differently at another time.
This gives rise to litigation. Do you recognize it even now? If you can recognize it, you may plow and weed as you please;
if you do not yet know it, you must continue to receive the offerings of devas and humans.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A tiger’s head sprouting horns—no one can manage it. Like sparks from flint and flashes of lightning, they must be spread thick and fast.

Even a hero would find it difficult; how could one who is dim-sighted skillfully evade them? Holding the sun and moon in his hands, carrying Mount Sumeru on his back, he hurls them toward the other quarters.
The sentient beings therein neither perceive nor know it; those sentient beings ride their donkeys right into the eyes of everyone."
[The Master] said, "All people are likewise unaware and unknowing. Do you understand? To offer this profound mind to the lands of all dust-motes—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
He ascended the hall and said: "Before a single bubble has arisen, before the ancient sail has set forth, the wind-signal has not come, and no one is rowing the oars. At this very moment..."
At such a time, how can one discern the course of the water? Have you not seen where the old man Yunmen extended his hand? Vast and clear waves leave no path for penetration.
Nor have you seen the elder of Huating leak his celestial secret: deep in the night, he returned alone, carrying the bright moon.
Do not wonder that we meet yet do not recognize one another; let it be so, for all eternity shall remain vast and dark.
Ascending the hall, he raised the teaching from the Middle Way: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them. The Master said: "What is the eye with which you all contemplate?
Those who possess this eye see that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as your own selves, are neither destroyed nor mixed. You all..."

Itself, together with the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, is neither destroyed nor mixed. Within it, there is not even so much as a speck of dust of the sages' dharma that acts as an obstruction to liberation;
nor is there even so much as a speck of dust of the ordinary person's dharma that constitutes unobstructed liberation. Can you still believe this?
If you can believe it, the ignorance and karmic consciousness are transformed into inexhaustible samādhi. If you cannot believe it, [the delusion remains].
Exhausting the samādhi, one returns to the karma-consciousness of ignorance.
Entering the hall, he said: "The wind sweeps away the lingering clouds; the universe is vast. The azure sky is like water, the moon is like a ring.
The Patriarch’s Heart-Seal is clearly present here; Facing this, you gentlemen, look closely."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The foolish person eliminates objects but does not forget the mind; the wise person forgets the mind but does not eliminate objects.

Not knowing that the nature of mind and objects is fundamentally suchness (tathatā), they encounter obstacles at every turn when meeting conditions before their eyes. He then raised his whisk and said: "Look!
This whisk has traveled to the Western Heavens and now returns to the land of Silla. Those who know me say I am dragging through mud and water; those who do not know me..."
This is to win a field of the bizarre. Entering the hall:
The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, free from all names and forms. Originally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings.

From where did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come? If you can utter a phrase that transcends the body, then how could it be divided that insentient things preach the Dharma? Is it not so?
[The Master] went up to the hall and said: "If you say that all dharmas are not [the Buddha-dharma], you blind the eyes of people of this time.

If you say that all dharmas are not non-[the Buddha-dharma], thorns grow upon level ground. Or if you say that all dharmas are precisely the Buddha-dharma, you are muddled and confused; it is not so."
This is right contemplation. It is the word that the sages of antiquity could not bring themselves to utter; to this day, no one has ever hit upon it.
If you can speak it, I will grant that you are a person who has understood the matter.

But if you cannot say anything at all, I know that even if you were to stay with me for thirty years, when the rain disperses and the clouds clear, heaven and earth will surely be revealed in their solitary brilliance.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I do not ask about 'the grass bowing and the wind blowing'; how is it regarding the matter beyond the Dharma-body?
The Master said: "The bird cries without shedding tears; the flower smiles without making a sound. The monk said:

"A single phrase transcends ten thousand ages. The Master said: "One must hear with one's eyes. The monk said: "Mañjuśrī does not sit upon the Golden Terrace Palace; he has his own freedom in the Nine Heavens."
Wancheng. The Master said, "Words are many; they lead one further away from the Way.
The monk bowed and said again, "In a forge, the amount of crude iron only increases; at the gate of a skilled physician, the number of patients grows ever greater.
It would be better to simply stop and rest. Moreover, the scenery within the flask is entirely present before you; for a moment, borrow the returning light to see it."
At that time, Chengxian ascended the hall and said: "If one wishes to recognize the principle of true emptiness, the True Suchness within the body pervades the external as well.
Sentient and insentient beings share a single essence; everywhere is identical to the True Dharma-realm. He then raised his whisk and said: "The whisk swallows up the dry [world]."
The *kun* hexagram is finished. From where do the myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images come?

If you can understand this, the Second Patriarch would not have gone to the Western Heaven and Bodhidharma would not have come to this Eastern Land. If you still do not understand, then who is it that returns to the hall right now?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When human beings dwell between heaven and earth, their nature contains a mixture of good and evil.
Once good and evil are mixed, discrimination arises; once discrimination has arisen, there is hatred and love. When there is hatred and love, there is grasping and rejecting;
when there is grasping and rejecting, there is coming and going; and when there is coming and going, there is birth and death. All of these are simply the affairs of human beings."
The common view is that this is not so; I, however, maintain it is otherwise. In the Dharma there is neither good nor evil, and fundamentally there is neither coming nor going.

If there is neither good nor evil, nor coming nor going, then there is no birth and death. Since there is neither birth nor death, how could good and evil be confused? How could coming and going be constrained?
If one can be thus, it may be said that though one does good all day long, one has never done good; though one does evil all day long, one has never done evil;
though one comes all day long, one has never come; though one goes all day long, one has never gone.
Is there anyone who clearly understands this principle? If you understand it, you will be able to grasp it, encountering its source at every turn. If you do not...
[The Master] says: "There is cold and heat that hastens your life; there are ghosts and spirits that envy your fortune.

He ascends the hall and cites the case of Mazu ascending the hall and Baizhang rolling up his mat. Later generations, failing to appreciate the source of this wind, all say that he left no trace behind.
Little do they realize that within the peach-blossom waves, it is precisely the right time to set sail; at the head of Qili Beach, it is even more worthy of praise.
Casting the line: Now there must be one who can distinguish between floating and sinking, who recognizes depth and shallowness. Step forward and let us examine the currents of the water.
Is there such a person? If not, then for now take up the fisherman’s flute and blow it idly by the seashore.
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "All numerical phrases—non-numerical phrases—what connection do they have with our numinous awareness?
Master Yunmen said, 'Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are numinous awareness. What, then, can be called a numerical phrase? The Master said, "Though gold dust is precious,"
If it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract. I am not like this. If you let it go, the source of spirit is a profound pool; let the solitary boat take its own course.
If you gather it back, the long is naturally long and the short is naturally short. Do you understand? Clouds return to Mount Hua, a thousand fathoms of white;
waters reach the Xiao and Xiang rivers, a single expanse of clarity.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "When it reflects in the eye, it is like the thousand suns; the myriad phenomena cannot escape its shadow and substance.
Ordinary people simply have not yet observed it; how can they disparage themselves and become disheartened? He then raised his whisk and said: "As for this—how do you observe it?
In seeing and hearing, there is only seeing and hearing; yet in seeing and hearing, one must not grasp at seeing and hearing."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Striking the void produces sound; who is the one who knows this? Striking an object produces no sound; it is all in vain to strain your ears.
This is not the Dharma of the present moment, so do not give rise to various thoughts. Arising and ceasing do not know one another; within this, there is neither front nor back.
Where the Elephant King walks, foxes and rabbits leave no tracks. When the moon in the water appears, wind and clouds are naturally distinct. Arriving here, heaven and earth are withdrawn."
It cannot be grasped. The universe does not know its name; a thousand sages stand downwind of it. Who dares speak of it head-on?
O virtuous ones, you should at once sweep away all your former livelihoods, your past deeds and activities, whether you understand them or not.
It would be better to take up your staff and return to the mountains, letting out a long啸 (shout) as the mist deepens.

Ascending the hall on the first day of the year: Time flows swiftly, its movements racing one after another. One exhales the old and inhales the new; having returned to the new, it once again becomes the old.

These illusory human affairs—what is there worth observing? Whether intoxicated or sober, whether singing or weeping, they are like wild horses flickering and galloping through the dust, or like fish in a parched rut, whose end is near. But tell me: how can one avoid falling into [this cycle]?
A single phrase of wind-and-rain brilliance—how would you say it? If one says it exists, looking for it, there is no form;
if one says it does not exist, calling out to it, there is sound. One does not know what this thing is; alas, the world competes headlong for it.

Ascending the hall, he said: "If we discuss this matter, to affirm it is to err; to deny it is to mistake it. To neither affirm nor deny is like an ant circling in a loop or a silkworm spinning its cocoon.
When you arrive here, it is like a great mass of fire: if you look upon it, it will burn away your very face."
It is not as if the turbid makes itself turbid, the clear makes itself clear, the bright makes itself bright, or the dark makes itself dark.
Every single thing is a possession of our own house; why must one ask for directions at the crossroads?

Ascending the hall: Samantabhadra’s practice and Mañjuśrī’s wisdom—on the slopes of Potalaka, a pure breeze arises. The crows cry and the sparrows chirp, entering directly through the faculty of hearing.
The grasses, trees, dust, and hairs—form and shadow mourn one another. Within sound there is no form; within form there is also no sound.
If sound and form interpenetrate, then everywhere there is neither before nor after. When the bird’s nest blew the cloth-hair, right here it was present.
The man withdrew. [The Master] then raised his whisk and said, "Tell me, how far apart are they? If you realize this after thirty years, do not say that I have degraded the noble to the lowly."

Ascending the hall: The lingering rain has just cleared, and a cool breeze gradually arises. This single breath is impartial; it acts, yet there is no acting. One might say the rice is ripe in the fields and the vegetables are green in the gardens;
this is entirely the style of a rustic home, the very foundation of a time of great peace. The superior men of the Five Lakes rest their heads high upon their pillows without worry;
they need not seek further, for their livelihood is manifest right now. If you would determine the ultimate meaning within these words: [The Master descended from the seat.]
The pivot of the occasion is revealed within a single phrase: a man waiting by a stump under the clear breeze and the moon; the dark hare grows distant as the spring grass turns green.
(With the whisk, he strikes the meditation seat and descends.)
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I have heard an ancient saying: 'If you obtain the root, do not worry about the branches.
What is this root? The Master said: "Simply recognize the interest within the lute; there is no need for the sound upon the strings. The monk asked: "What are the branches? The Master said:

"The green mountains do not obstruct the flying white clouds. The monk said: "I have already received the Master’s instruction on the root and the branches. As for the matter of the ultimate vehicle, what of it?"
"What? the Master said. "Only at nightfall does one see the needle piercing the person. He spoke again:
"The image in a mirror may be said to exist, yet grasping it does not fill the hand. The image in a mirror may be said to be non-existent, yet it is as distinct as a formal portrait.
Therefore, it cannot be grasped, nor can it be discarded; within this very 'unobtainability,' there is simply obtaining. Do you understand?"
He did not act like Vimalakīrti, yet he resembled Fu Dashi. He ascended the hall and said:
"The year is nearly spent, yet we already see the onset of mid-spring. Days and months race by; prosperity and decline alternate.
Human life is but this—cease further agitation. I observe that the past, having already gone, cannot be pursued; the future, yet to come, [cannot be grasped]."
"You may ask: 'Right now there is no abiding; where can one search? O people, how is it that you lose this priceless treasure in the pit of the sense bases (*āyatana*)?
You do not realize that the path to the blue clouds lies right before your eyes.
If you continue to run about seeking it, your confusion will only increase. Now tell me, where is the beginning of the road? He then raised his whisk and said, "It is right here."
A person of keen faculties: upon seeing [the Master] once, they immediately request to stride alone through the crimson heavens.
Entering the hall, he said: "If you do not see me for three days, do not regard me as I was before.
If you regard me as I was before, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth will deceive you. How can you avoid being deceived? Whether there is profit or loss, it does not depart from walking."
In the city, a cow from Huai Prefecture eats the grain; yet rice in Luoling is expensive. Singing a long song, I shall go back home;
pure breezes fill my eyes, stirring heaven and earth.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The patterns of tigers and leopards cannot help but shine brightly compared to those of dogs and sheep;
the luster of gold and jade cannot help but dazzle compared to that of tiles and stones; and the enlightened person cannot help but awaken the masses of the deluded.

Once these three conditions are complete, then one must surely overflow the heavens, capable of becoming the vast ocean; one must surely be towering and lofty, capable of becoming a mountain range."—Master Xiou.

O person! A man of clear enlightenment and eminent discernment, who has long harbored a sharp brilliance yet refrained from seeking contemporary fame—my hope is that you will not conceal your radiance nor hide your functional utility.
Only by unrolling the sutra scrolls from within the dust can one truly be called a "person who unties the cords.
Thus, may the auspicious sprouts and extraordinary herbs cause every leaf to waft forth fragrance; may the phoenixes and qilins ensure every cry resonates in harmony. If you can act in this way...
This may be called the re-illumination of my Way; future generations have hope. (At this assembly, the Head Seat Xiù was appointed as a monk.
Ascending the hall for the Imperial Birthday: Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil;
the Sovereign attains the One and brings order to the world. Once the world is ordered, all lands submit; once all lands submit, the myriad states present their tribute.
When the myriad states have all presented their tribute, the people will no longer engage in strife. When the people do not engage in strife, they likewise will not commit theft.
When there is neither theft nor strife, wind and rain will naturally become harmonious. Once wind and rain are harmonious, the world will be in great tranquility.
When the world is settled in peace, you must sing this single melody of Great Peace; do not seek it within hearing by recognizing what is not heard.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All that has been done prior to the fifteenth day is like a single night’s dream.
Flying about for a hundred years, after the fifteenth day, all things have not yet sprouted; one gradually begins to dream. This very day, the fifteenth, is precisely dreaming within a dream.
Is there anyone here who can trace the origin of this dream? Come forth and try to discern the good and the ill. Liang.
Jiur said: "To distinguish the master amidst the dust is not yet considered difficult; however, among ten thousand who do not know how to read or write, there is not even one.
When the drum sounds cease as you enter the hall, I allow for a moment of composure; yet if you further burn incense, it already constitutes a foreboding sign.
Nevertheless, even so, this will weary you, Senior Monk; come, let us take another look."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The lush spring grasses clearly reveal the celestial mechanism; the distinct cries of the cuckoo are entirely the realm of Samantabhadra.

It would be better to cease all military expeditions and put an end to war. Moreover, with the wind and rain being harmonious and the seas and rivers tranquil, lay down your spears and halberds and sit securely at home. Be careful and heedful."
Ascending the hall: I have a single phrase; I hand it over with my own hands. A blink of an eye, a raising of an eyebrow—this applies to both the Western Heaven and this land.
Ascending the hall: The mind is the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma. How would Huanglong dare to press the noble into the lowly?

If there were dharmas or an original mind, it would not be mind and it would not be the fundamental dharma. The myriad Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust would dissolve like crumbling walls or melting ice. All...
Where do you intend to look for the Patriarch? Each of you, please return to the hall. Entering the hall:
Where the sound of the bell ceases, the sound of the drum continues; where the sound of the drum ceases, every dharma is perfectly realized.
If one further raises the discussion of bodhi and nirvana, or true thusness and liberation, these are all untimely words. One need only attain the clouds and mists...
When the clouds disperse, the solitary moon shines of itself; when sand and gravel are removed, the true gold reveals itself of itself.
Entering the hall: Every person holds the pearl of the divine serpent; every household embraces the raw jade of Mount Jing.
Whether walking, sitting, acting, or responding—this single segment of radiance has never been interrupted. Take care.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "If one clarifies only the self but does not awaken to what is before one's eyes, this person has eyes but no feet.
If one awakens to what is before one's eyes but does not clarify the self, this person has feet but no eyes. According to these two types of people, throughout the twelve hours of the day,"
There has always been one thing stored within my breast. Since this thing resides in my breast, the signs of its unease are constantly before my eyes.
Being thus before my eyes, it creates obstructions wherever I go. How can I attain peace and stability? Did not the Patriarch say:
"To grasp it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path; to let it go naturally, its essence is without coming or dwelling"?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way has no substance; it is because of the Way that it receives a name. A name has no inherent name; it is because of the name that a designation is established.
He then raised his whisk and said: "You must not call this a whisk. What would you call it? Today, Huanglong has been thoroughly exposed by you all."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Do not cherish the holy; 'holy' is but an empty name. Do not loathe the mundane; 'mundane' is falsely established.
If you can simply exhaust all attachments to the holy and the mundane, the true and eternal will naturally manifest its essence. Can you still believe this? If you can believe it, then proceed."

It is not improper to say that within the midst of one's study and practice, there may be some degree of correspondence [with the truth]. If your faith does not reach this level, you might still be considered a man of stature.
Upon ascending the hall: beneath the forested body, all things fall into ruin; yet, I am grateful that the venerable superiors do not judge me solely by outward appearances.
You have come from a thousand li away; we have gathered here through long-standing ties. My only concern is that during this time there has been no further hospitality to extend.

I have only this single branch of a whisk to express my sincere devotion. It makes no distinction between high and low, nor does it differentiate between noble and humble; at times, it transforms the raw into the ripe.
At times it transforms the ripe into the raw; at other times it is bland, empty, and sparse, rather than possessing a hundred flavors.

Yet, being able to satisfy one's hunger once allows one to suddenly forget a hundred prior famines. Thus, one avoids the sight of borrowing and owing others' wealth, or consuming another's food and drink at improper times.
To those who know me, I am seen as one who brandishes his whip while lamenting his own shadow; to those who do not know me, I merely win a bout of bitter acridity.
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no mind that can be attained; what is spoken cannot be called the Dharma. The Master said: "The gate of the Patriarchs has already been flung open.
A pair of mandarin ducks has been embroidered; let you all gaze at it as you please. But tell me, where does the golden needle fall?"
He spoke again: "If you realize that the mind is not the mind, only then will you understand the mind and its mental factors. Do you understand?
A clap of thunder from the South Mountain lightly awakens the slumbering insects from head to tail."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Who is without mind? Whose mind is without Buddha? The Buddha is always present within people; it is people who are constantly chasing after external objects.
Right now, when you see forms and hear sounds, are these objects or are they not? If they are not objects, then at the very moment you see a form—"
One cannot fail to call it "form" when seeing form; one cannot fail to call it "sound" when hearing sound.
But if these are all merely material things, how can one explain the ultimate principle? Without clarifying the Seal of the Mind-ground, it is difficult to pass through Zhaozhou’s Barrier.
Ascending the hall: Round reflections race one another as we approach the early summer. Flowers bloom and fall; things remain, yet people change.
Yesterday it shone upon youthful faces; today it shines upon white-haired heads. Between white hair and youthful faces, the distance is but a few inches.
Do you know of anything that does not partake in the cycles of cold and heat?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When the master craftsman has not yet appeared, jade and stone remain undistinguished; when the skilled smelter is absent, gold and sand are mixed together.
Is there anyone here who has attained self-awakening without a teacher? Come forth and discern this for me! He then raised his whisk and said: "Tell me, is this gold or is it sand?
'If you see it and do not take it, you will regret it a thousand miles away.'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schemed or measured. It is high and without superior; vast and beyond limit. It is deep and without bottom;
profound and unfathomable. Greatly it encompasses heaven and earth; minutely it enters the infinitesimal gaps.
For this reason, the ancients proclaimed the fundamental principle and exerted their meritorious efforts. You all should try to discern and clarify this."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is not a solitary standard, nor is it without companions. Those who do not recognize it are still muddled;
those who do recognize it are likewise crude and confused. Not knowing what kind of thing it is, it is thus difficult to discern.
Were it not for the Golden-Colored Dhūta, there would be no place even for reason to clear the debt."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wind whistles and the leaves fall; The wild geese do not come, and news is scarce.
No one blows the tune for returning home; It leaves me clapping my hands in vain hesitation."
He spoke again: "This single melody is neither metal, stone, silk, nor bamboo; it is also not gourd, clay, leather, or wood.

It is heard yet not heard, seen yet not seen. I do not know what kind of tune this is. Behold the time when wind and clouds meet; there will surely be those who understand its true sound throughout the Five Lakes."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Now, the profound Way cannot be attained through the performance of merit; the sagely wisdom cannot be known through a conscious mind;
the True Dharma cannot be realized through the preservation of 'I'; and the ultimate achievement cannot be produced through the management of affairs.

When the ancients responded to the illness with medicine for a single occasion, it was not because they were so; rather, if one is a man of integrity, upon emerging from seclusion, one shall bring order to the world."
If you do not emerge from below, I will roll it up and keep it within my breast. If you are consistently harmonious in sound and compliant in resonance, I shall cast you out in all directions.
If you manifest yourself in wine shops and brothels, I shall sleep alone on a solitary peak. Now tell me:
where is the eye through which Huanglong acts for the benefit of others?
Ascending the hall: The new thunder has already burst forth, yet the cuckoo has not yet cried. The mountain clouds are hazy and thin; the river grasses grow lush and green.
The golden crow emerges from the sea; the jade hare sinks in the west. Whether heard or seen, who awakens and who remains deluded? The old man Lu does not know where he has gone;
his robe and bowl are transmitted in vain at Caoxi.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When seeing the very act of seeing, that which sees is not itself seeing. Seeing is already detached from seeing; even seeing cannot reach it. Is there still a place to turn about?
If you can turn it, before your eyes there is no disciple, and upon this seat there is no old monk.
If you cannot turn it, do not let your idle scholarly interpretations bury the mind of the Patriarch. Be careful!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Throughout the long night and clear evening, what is there to do? The Buddha-nature is the jewel of the precepts, the seal upon the mind-ground.
Mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the garments upon the body. But when the clouds and mists have dissipated, where does the body abide?
After a long silence, he said: "The snow is cold. Return to the hall and warm yourselves by the fire."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wisdom of all-encompassing penetration is free from obstruction; mountains, rivers, and stone walls pass through it as if they were people.

You do not realize that this is neither a marvelous exercise of supernatural power nor some other technique; it is simply what you all use in your daily lives. Why, then, do you speak of 'understanding' and 'not understanding'?
It is only because your minds harbor notions of victory and defeat and you have not shed your attachments to what is seen and heard. When these perceptions suddenly arise—"
The moon in the water: these two are mutually dependent and thus constitute distinct phenomena.

If you now wish to understand this easily, you must completely clear away all your former worldly occupations until they are utterly exhausted. Only when your thousand eyes suddenly open will you finally meet with me at that time.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All that has form is entirely illusory. Do you see this Dharma Hall? If you see it, then there are phenomena outside the mind;
if you do not see it, then your eyes are impaired. How else would you understand this? After a long silence, he said: "Carry your poems and books back to your old retreat;
wild flowers and singing birds are one and the same spring."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "The great ocean has a pearl that cannot be sought; I beg the Master to grant it from beneath the chin of Huanglong.
The Master said, "When people are level, they do not speak; when water is level, it does not flow. The monk said, "Is it not this very thing? Or is there something else? The Master said, [silently].
If a single word misses the mark, a thousand words will not be used. The monk said, "In this vast universe there are countless people, yet only the barbarian monk smiles and nods his head.
The Master said, "Even at the very summit of Long Peak, one must arrive there in person before it can be attained."

He spoke again: "The ultimate discourse of the Buddha-dharma is not something achieved through clever speech or sharp rhetoric, nor is it something obtained through supernatural powers or meditative realization.
Even if one were to take the entire universe and the great earth and present them all as a single question, one would only gain a field of frivolous debate, which leads further away from the Way.
The Patriarch came from the West solely to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one may become a Buddha; he did not [seek anything else]."

The establishment of written characters, and even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, is like using yellow leaves to make imitation gold coins to temporarily stop a child’s crying.
The Great Way is fundamentally empty and still; it requires no contrivance. Perfectly profound and pervasive throughout the ten directions of space, how could it have any fixed location?
Yet now, because you do not understand, you perceive only the discerning awareness before your eyes, leading to the two divergent paths of clarity and obscurity. Thus you listen [to the teachings].
They utter sounds, yet their vision does not transcend form. Such faults and afflictions are truly pitiable; they fail to realize this, mistaking a thief for their own son.
Therefore, when a high-minded seeker of the profound reaches this point, they must look directly within themselves: "How should one handle the matters that have come down from of old?
Ultimately, what will one use to confront birth and death? Do not harbor a mind of deluded conceptualization.
I shall decide for myself; let this suffice for my entire life and serve as my ultimate goal.

When another time comes, on the day my life ends, my consciousness will be in turmoil and I will have no foundation to rely upon—by then, what will regret avail? Why not simply settle the matter right here and now?
Without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, in the space of a single finger-snap, one can transcend the wondrous Vairocana Flower Treasury.
The Ocean of Adornments—down to the very lifting and lowering of the feet—is entirely the realm of the great beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Is this not a source of lifelong joy and the aspiration of a true man? How much more so within this gate, where everything is the original reality inherent in all people;
it is not attained through cultivation or realization, nor is it obtained from others. You must quickly realize this, cast off the sense bases and their objects, and exhaust [all delusions].
To the limit of the future, one shall attain and forever maintain this, never again falling away.
If one can act in this way, they may be called a shaven-headed monk in saffron robes who prolongs the Buddha’s life; if it is otherwise, such a thing is impossible.
Xie Tongyi, the Pacification Commissioner of Changsha, requested that the Master ascend the seat at Beichan.
After the Master had finished offering incense, he sat cross-legged. A monk asked: "‘This very mind is Buddha’—in these times, this has not yet entered the profound mystery.
‘Neither mind nor Buddha’—this is still merely pointing out the tracks. As for the ultimate path beyond the previous, which the thousand sages have not transmitted—"
"Master, how do you benefit people today? The Master said, "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. The monk said, "In that case, when the dragon obtains water, his spirit increases;
when the tiger encounters the mountains, his majesty grows fierce. The Master said, "One must believe that the sun and moon within the alchemical vessel are long-lasting.
The monk said, "The One Qi does not speak, yet it contains all forms; where can the myriad spirits offer thanks for its impartiality?"
The Master said, "When meeting people, do not misrepresent [the teaching]. A monk asked, "Why do all the sages of the past not arrive here?
The Master said, "What place is this? The monk said, "In that case, when the curtain is rolled up, one sees the whole world.
The Master said, "What about the affairs of the world? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "He knows only one side of it."
Not knowing the second [line]. A monk asked: "In the past, when Li Ao ascended Mount Yaoqiao, he said, 'The clouds are in the blue sky;
the water is in the jar. Today, Tongyi stands before the precious seat; I beg the Master for a single phrase to settle the lineage. The Master said:
"When there is no wind upon the pond, the waves subside of themselves. The monk asked: "Is there still a point of realization? The Master said: "How would you realize it?"
The monk said, "The golden sun soars far beyond the azure heavens; when the jade hare shines, the four seas are clear.
The Master said, "It would be better to step back and look. The monk said, "The assembly bears witness; this student bows in thanks."
The Master said: "The Way of the Patriarchs cannot be observed through physical forms or vessels, nor can it be fathomed by the conscious mind.
Every question and every answer is an offering of the Dharma; yet within the realm of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), these do not constitute the final realization.

As for the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, they are like describing food to someone who has never tasted it. Since one relies on another's description of the food, the essential point lies within oneself."
Taste it for oneself. Once one has tasted it personally, one can then discern its flavor—whether it is sweet or pungent, salty or bland.
The coming of Bodhidharma from the West to point directly at the human mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha is likewise so.
Since true nature is manifested through words and texts, that nature must be personally witnessed by oneself. If one can witness it personally, one will then be able to understand it fully.

At present, regarding what is real and what is delusory, and what constitutes birth and death—if one can thoroughly understand reality, delusion, birth, and death, then looking back upon all language and texts, one will see that they are merely conventional expressions and possess no ultimate meaning. Yet, at this moment, one does not yet understand this.
Where does the illness lie? It lies in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. It arises from failing to know, as it truly is, the destination of the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi).

One clings to this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as one's own vision; yet one fails to realize that these seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all exist because of the external objects before them.
If those external objects and realms did not exist, then this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing would be just like [the eyes of] a tortoise.
The fur of a rabbit and the horns of a hare have no place of return. Having no place of return, one becomes a wanderer.

Once one has become a wanderer, then every thought-moment shifts and passes away; the new does not stop, just as fire turns to ash, gradually wasting away. This process of wasting away does not cease.
It is certain that this body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction. Therefore, one dies here and is born there; dies there and is born here. Birth after birth, death after death;
death after death, birth after birth—one receives retribution according to karma throughout the six realms and four modes of birth.

One changes heads and faces, taking on forms or being formless, having four feet, two feet, many feet, or no feet. Thus one takes birth and thus one receives retribution, like drawing water from a well.
The well-wheel: one rises while the other falls. O worthy ones, at such a time, how will you support and regulate it?
Since you are great men, you must know there is the business of a great man. Now that you know there is the business of a great man, how will you understand it?
Is there a place where you can understand it? If there is no place where you can understand it, then today Huanglong cannot help but stir up the wind and raise the waves.
Waves. He beats his oars and raises his sail, then lifts his whisk and says: "Look! Only the firm and dense body manifests within all atoms.

Do you see it? The whisk is an atom; where is the firm and dense body? If you can see it here, then the myriad Buddhas of the finest dust and their hundreds of thousands of samādhis will all be clearly understood in a single snap of the fingers. Thus one is able to...
Entering water, one does not drown; entering fire, one is not burned. One becomes many; the many become one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears.

Even the heavens and hells, tiger dens and demon palaces, the moonlit glades and breezy courtyards, the brothels and wine shops—all these are places where people establish their dwellings and sustain their lives. If one can act in this manner, one may truly be called a great man.

He is well able to emerge from life and enter death, attaining great mastery. Even if he has not yet turned [the wheel of dharma], the crane’s leg is naturally long and the duck’s leg is naturally short;
he can answer questions on behalf of others within his chamber.
The Master once asked a monk, "The whale waves are vast and boundless; fish and dragons vie for their might. How do you raise your sails and lift your oars? The monk had no reply.
[The Master] provided the answer on his behalf, saying, "I simply watch. He further provided another answer on his behalf, saying, "Entering the water, one sees the tall man."
Someone asked: "To cite one is to clarify the three; those who know this will not come. Thirty years hence, another set of rules will be substituted. He replied on their behalf:
"Do not let them be subjected to such hardship."
One day he asked a monk, "The qilin is not an auspicious omen; the juetsuo is not a spiritual marvel. When the four seas are peaceful and clear, who will present tribute?
A monk of the time replied, "Receive one ox from a person, and return one horse to a person. He also asked another monk, "Seizing and holding fast the heavens and earth."

The eyes are full and the mouth speaks, yet one cannot distinguish the *gong* and *shang* musical scales. What kind of person is this? [A master] provided the answer: "One who does not spare body or life. Or at times he asked:
"The great man who is unstained by the dust of the world—does he still enter with a burden, or does he leave it behind? How can this be?"
The principle of not harming things departed. A successor said, "It emerges levelly.
One day he asked a monk, "It was before me; suddenly it is behind me. Tell me, what thing is so difficult to discern?
If you can discern it, calamity will not enter the door of a prudent house. If you cannot discern it, then today at Huanglong—"
"Obtaining life from within death. Another provided a substitute response: "How very leisurely! Yet another provided a substitute response: "If you want it, then speak. Someone once asked:
"If there were no spring breeze, the flowers would not bloom; do you recognize this yet? A substitute response was given: "I know.
Yet another provided a substitute response: "Planting rice, one should not produce bean sprouts."
At another time, he was asked: "Dust has no self-nature; it is established by gathering the Truth. What is this matter that is established?
He then raised his whisk and said, "The myriad Buddhas of a single speck of dust and their hundreds of thousands of samādhis are all contained herein.

It would be better to awaken to this. Is there anyone who can awaken? Someone spoke on his behalf, saying, "The one who loses his life is caught on the hook. Another spoke on his behalf, saying, "A transgression."
He asked the assembly, "The ten directions have no walls, and the four sides have no gates. Old Guankui cannot even breathe out;
why do you not meet him within the flames? He spoke on his behalf, saying, "Many laugh at me."
Sometimes he was asked [a question]. Upon encountering clarity, it was immediately obscured. At such a time as this, it is difficult to distinguish the refined from the coarse.
You must know there is a phrase that startles people. On his behalf, he said: "Look after three days."

At another time, he asked: "When auspicious snow falls, it portends a bountiful year; when the golden wind blows, the withered grass turns. Within the Buddha-dharma, how does one distinguish between gain and loss?
He provided the verse in response: "The sorrowful man knows the night is long. He asked again: "To achieve both at once without concealment—does anyone find this unsatisfactory?
Come forward and speak! He provided the verse in response: "It should have fallen to me."
Sometimes he would ask a question, and once he had spoken it, he would not say it again. When asked, "The child is spoiled by his wealthy family; where did he go to pluck the willow blossoms?
Bring me word of this," he replied on his behalf: "Without one matter, it is difficult to grow one bit of wisdom."

At another time, he was questioned: "Your ministers are as numerous as raindrops and your fierce generals as thick as clouds. With painted halberds arrayed before your gate, how will you issue your commands?
He replied: "The seal of authority is in my hand. He asked again: "Tents are pitched and nets are spread; not even water can pass through.
Tell me, where would birds and beasts fall? He replied: "I know well that they left their homes too early."
Question: "A single leaf falls and the world turns autumn; it pierces the eyes of the monks. The Buddha Hall enters the lantern—what level of capacity is this?
In his stead, he said: "The strength of one’s attainment is not equal to meeting the right time."
One day he asked a monk, "When looking inward, one does not see oneself; when listening back, one hears nothing of oneself. How do you discern this?
He spoke on his behalf, saying, "Each time it is raised, it is new once more. He asked again, "If you can encompass it horizontally in a single phrase, then speak from your own perspective.
Why is it that spring is performing the ordinances of autumn? The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*) and said, "What can be done about this? The Master said, "It is like..."
[The Master] acted as if picking up a rabbit; the rabbit, too, was not encountered. A substitute said, "One with eyes. [The Master] sometimes asked:
"To see the Buddha by brushing away the dust—this is no extra effort. Furthermore, if one were to brandish a sword, would there not be at least one or half a person on the crossroads?
The substitute said, "Having a head but no tail makes one loathed by others."
Someone asked: "The knot is half-loosened; break it into three and hang it toward the wall. I will spread it out with you, so bring me one question.
The substitute said: "Why must there be one? He asked again: "Great wisdom is beyond names; true emptiness leaves no trace.
If you were to instruct on breaking through [delusion], I fear this would not be the way of a good person. The substitute said: "We must not let each other down."
Sometimes he asked: "The Buddha-dharma does not require study; it gives rise to a refreshing breeze wherever one looks. This is the view of ordinary people. How would you respond?
He provided the answer on their behalf: "How can anyone blame me? He also provided another answer on their behalf: "A dragon's head and a snake's tail."
Someone asked: "If you are within the lines, we will bind and kill you; if you are outside the lines, we will chase and kill you.
Without leaving this space, try to explain yourself clearly. He replied on behalf of [the master]: "Please do so. He was asked again: "The clouds and moon remain exactly as they are."

The mountain streams and peaks still have their differences; cast aside that which is right before one’s eyes. Where can one settle the matter? [The Master] provides the verse: "A single arrow brings down two vultures. Sometimes he asks:
"When I press my finger, the Ocean Seal emits light; from where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come? [The Master] provides the verse: [As above].
He said, "One is already too many. He then spoke on behalf [of the master], saying, "How can you deny it?
He asked a monk, "Whether coming from the south or going to the north, let us leave that aside for now; why did you lean your staff against the old man Xuansha?
He spoke on behalf [of the monk], saying, "He shook his sleeves and went out."
Someone asked: "The wind does not come, so the tree does not move; the rushing stream passes beneath the blade—please, briefly, let us meet. He spoke on his behalf, saying:
"Consider that I am old."
Once, someone asked: "The waters of the four great oceans are upon your head, and Mount Sumeru is beneath your feet;
where can the creatures of the scales and feathers hide their bodies? A substitute replied: "How could one ever stuff a person's mouth shut?"

He asked the assembly: "When one maneuvers strategy within the tent and establishes the boundaries of a realm, and when the ranked officers are granted their fiefs, how are these distinctions to be made? The assembly replied:
"Upon the tips of the hundred grasses."
Someone asked: "When incense and rotten onions are placed in the same vessel, and water and milk are mixed in a single jar, how can one distinguish them while they are still hanging from the hand?
The Master replied on his behalf: "Noble Youth’s staff."
Sometimes he asked: "When the wind is at sea and the boat is on the mountain, why did the ancients fail to leap out? He provided the verse-response:
"It is difficult to assume the appearance of a Great Man."

Someone asked: "Where is the eye when the light of the eyes shines everywhere, leaking through every point? If you set aside the pure water pitcher, where is the eye? [The Master] answered on his behalf:
"Where are the Buddha-dharma, the body, and the mind? He also said: "To remain unharmed when facing a precipice is simply one's fundamental duty;
this is what Xuefeng meant when he said, 'I will leave it for another time. [The Master] answered on his behalf: "I have never falsely accused anyone."
He asked the assembly: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. The ancients have already said this; I do not want it. Return to me the first tally!
He spoke on behalf [of the assembly], saying: "It is so. He asked again: "You say 'it is so'—how about that? He spoke on behalf [of the assembly], saying: [It is so.]
A son does not speak of his father’s virtues.

Someone asked this; [the Master] replied, "The mouth is only fit for eating rice; even a monk with clear eyes does not know its breath. On behalf of the questioner, he said: "I dare not exceed my lot."
Once, when asked, “When one recognizes the occasion and discerns the stars, where does the fault lie? he replied in his stead, “By the time you realize it was a mistake.
Again, when asked, “To regret not being careful at the beginning is like drawing a bow after the thief has fled,” he replied in his stead, “Not even a trace of it remains.”

Someone asked: "When one raises the intention, one immediately knows there is [something]. Who is it that thoroughly understands this? He answered on behalf [of the Master]: "The bystander. He asked a monk:
"To emerge from within the gate, the fault lies with those of the present age; to exit from within the body, do not let those of the present age pass through.
How is this? He answered on behalf [of the Master]: "It is difficult to laugh at or find it strange. He further answered on behalf [of the Master]: "A barrier."
Someone asked: "Thorny brambles do not grow; why is it so difficult for them to become great beams and rafters? He replied: "It is because one compares oneself to others.
The questioner asked again: "Do not go beyond what is necessary; examine this closely. He replied: "Within the Way of benevolence and righteousness."
Once, a monk entered while the Elder Huanglong was absent. The monk said, "I am carrying stolen goods and crying out for injustice.
The Master said, "Finished. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his whisk.
Someone asked: "I understand the line 'I know it, but you, my relative, do not drown in it. But how about the line 'light and dark are not distinguished'?
He answered on his behalf: "The previous part was still tolerable. He asked again: "When encountering the base, one is noble. What thing comes in such a way? He answered on his behalf: [Silence].
"It must come to this. Again, he spoke on their behalf, saying: "Alas!
One day he saw a monk and said, 'Today my mouth is hanging on the wall. The monk replied, "The heart of a thief is always filled with trepidation."
The Master struck once with his whisk. The monk said, "I thank you, Reverend, for your repeated kindness. The Master said, "To gain an advantage is to fall into a disadvantage.
In his room, he cited an ancient precedent.
Case: At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a single flower.
Kāśyapa smiled. The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. The Master said:
"To have pierced right through the skull is already to have changed one's eyes. When facing the brink of death, there is no need for alarm. Where can you find the old Śākyamuni?"
The Master raised the case of Jingqing asking a monk, "What is that sound outside the door? The monk said, "The sound of raindrops falling. Jingqing said, "Sentient beings are inverted;
deluded about themselves, they pursue external objects. The monk asked, "How about you, Master? Jingqing said, "I have not even reached the point of being deluded about myself. The monk said, "..."
"Since you have not lost your way, what is your meaning? Qing said, "To leave one's body may still be easy; to shed one's entire being to realize the Way should be difficult.
The Master said, "Speaking of difficulty and ease only serves to further confuse yourself. To ensure you do not lose your way, if you were to try to call out right now, what sound would it be?"
The Master cited a monk’s question to Deshan: “Caoshan spoke of the moon; Lingyan pointed to the moon. I do not ask about that. What is the moon?
Deshan said, “Last night at the third watch, it turned toward the west. The monk was speechless. The Master said:
“He was even more quick-witted! You should have simply told him: ‘A true spiritual friend—only a sage can truly know existence and know non-existence.’”
Daci raised his staff and said to the assembly, "I, this mountain monk, cannot answer questions; I simply recognize the illness. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed.
Daci immediately returned to his quarters. The Master said, "What a pity he was let go! Had I seen him just as he stepped out, I would have struck him across the back with my staff.
Had I waited for him to realize where the blow had come from, he would have avoided [the cycle of] ten thousand ages."
Below. When one encounters such critical examination, even Huanglong today recognizes the illness and knows how to respond.
Suppose, however, a man were to come forth and overturn the rope bed—how would you handle that? I ask you, Senior, please try to provide a substitute phrase for this.
A monk asked Nan-yuan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Nan-yuan said, "Neither up to heaven nor into hell.
The monk asked, "What about you, Master? Nan-yuan said, "Do you know where Old Bao-ying has fallen?"
The monk hesitated. The Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk. He then called the monk forward, saying, "It is precisely for you to act.
He struck him again with the whisk. The Master said: "Even a flaw in white jade can still be polished away;
yet when the illness has reached the vital organs, one must still seek treatment. Since the Master’s command is already in your hands, why do you not act? Where does the fault lie?"
Case: A monk asked Xinghua, "What is it like when [the wind] comes from the four quarters and the eight directions? Xinghua said, "I strike the one in the center.
The monk bowed. Xinghua said, "Yesterday, I went to attend a village vegetarian feast. On my way back, midway along the road, I was struck by—"
A violent wind and torrential rain arose. [The Master] went to an ancient temple and managed to take shelter there. The Master asked a monk, "Do you understand?
The monk said, "I do not. The Master said, "I have a verse: One is not, two is not yet formed; a warbling oriole amidst falling blossoms and fragrant grasses.
Rain ceases in the quiet courtyard, the night is just beginning to settle; a sliver of moon rises once more from the sea."
He cited the conversation between Grand Master Lu Xun and Nanquan. Having mentioned Dharma Master Zhao’s words, “Heaven and earth share the same root as I;
