the myriad things are one body with me,” which are indeed most extraordinary, Nanquan pointed to the flowers in front of the courtyard and said to the Grand Master:
People of that time saw this single stalk of flowers as if it were a dream. The Master asked a monk, "When Nanquan spoke thus, how did he perceive the oneness of all things and myself?
The monk raised his sitting cloth (zuoju). The Master said, "Raising it is easy."
It is difficult to see it return. Atop Mount Sumeru, the celestial winds are cold; towering and steep, it descends straight toward the Dragon’s Cave. Who would dare even look upon it?
A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the True Dharma Eye? Yunmen said, “Universal. The Master said, “Say one more word!”
"Blind! For now, let us both manage to see each other.
Xushan asked a monk, "Have you ever been to Xuefeng? The monk replied, "I have been there. Xushan said, "When I went there previously, matters were not yet sufficient.
How are things now? The monk said, "Now they are sufficient. Xushan said, "Sufficient for porridge."
“Sufficient rice,” the monk replied, remaining silent. Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying, “Sufficient porridge, sufficient rice.
The Master said, “That is so, but it nonetheless lacks the principle of the Buddha-dharma. A monk asked, “How is it that there is no principle of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master instead asked the monk, “What do you usually use to eat your porridge and rice? The monk said, “I use my mouth to eat. The Master shouted, “The pillar!”
"Why? Because you are full. If you were to chew through a single grain of rice, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth would deceive you.
[The Master] cited Master Yunmen, who took up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "This staff transforms into a dragon and swallows up heaven and earth.
From where could the mountains, rivers, and the great earth have come? The Master said: "A master of clear eyes; even to this day..."
It still remains. Suddenly, if there were a man who came forth and said, "This is the staff;
what fault is there in the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? I would grant that he possesses a single eye.
Citing an episode where Deshan once visited Longtan, [Xuedou] said: "For a long time I have heard of Longtan;
yet when I arrived, the pond was not to be seen and the dragon did not appear. Longtan said, "You have come personally to Longtan. Xuedou remarked, "Taking a mistake for a mistake.
The Master asked, "In Xuedou’s saying this, one does not know whether it is Deshan taking a mistake for a mistake, or Longtan taking a mistake for a mistake."
A mistake is indeed a mistake. A monk who recognizes good and ill fortune must know where to go. Those who have not yet passed through the barrier should also discern this clearly.
Do you understand this thoroughly? Even if you manage to cultivate it, it will not be timber fit for a pillar.
I cite the Middle Way of the Teachings: "Therefore, if you now establish knowing and seeing upon [the basis of] knowing and seeing, this is the very root of ignorance.
If knowing and seeing are themselves without seeing, this is Nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could there be room for any other thing within this? The Master said:
"The entire universe and the great earth are all the eyes of the Venerable One. There is not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction. It is simply what you see right now."
When seeing, see only; when hearing, hear only; when acting, act only; when sitting, sit only. Remain entirely unmoved and unattached.
If you were to become attached, I would have already gone to the Western Heaven this morning and returned to the Eastern Land by evening.
Citing the Way of the former sages: "Birth-and-death and bodhi—these two are certainly existent dharmas. If one harbors doubt regarding this, one is deaf and blind, lacking the eye of wisdom.
Furthermore, it says: "Birth-and-death and bodhi—these two are certainly non-existent dharmas.
If one harbors doubt regarding this, one is deaf and blind, lacking the eye of wisdom. The Master asked: "Are these two the same, or are they contradictory, or should they be considered distinct?"
There is a principle here. Try to decide it for yourself.
To illustrate, Master Yunmen one day asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Jiangxi. Yunmen said:
"How many straw sandals have you worn out? The monk did not answer.
The Master said, "Master Yunmen has already displayed the markings of a tiger or leopard, yet he unconsciously fell into this monk's pitfall.
Is there anyone now who can lift Yunmen up? Speak a turning word, and you shall meet Huanglong. He asked, "What would that word be?"
"Generating the Path.
[The Master] cited the verse by Hanshan: "I have heard of Śākyamuni Buddha, but I do not know where he is.
When I contemplate his whereabouts, he is nowhere other than my own site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The Master said: "What kind of contemplation is this? Where is Old Śākya? Try [to find out]."
One must certainly look at it.
[The Master] cited Emperor Tongguang. One day, while sitting with Xinghua, the Emperor asked, "I have acquired a treasure from Central China, yet there is no one to appraise its value.
Xinghua said, "Let me borrow Your Majesty’s treasure for a moment. The Emperor then opened his bundle.
[The monk] offered his head and feet. Huazhou said, "This is the treasure of a sovereign; who would dare to set its price?
The Master said, "Although Xinghua acted according to the occasion at that time, how could he avoid burying the 'Son of Heaven' for a day? Had I been Xinghua at that moment..."
I simply say this to him: "The precious oyster and clam have been acquired, yet they are of no use;
let him find another means of livelihood hereafter, so as to avoid being ridiculed by onlookers. Now, if someone were suddenly to ask you, Venerable Sir, how would you appraise them?

The Master cited a monk asking Xuan Sha: "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are not needed; what is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Xuan Sha replied:
"The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all unnecessary. The Master said: "It is like a pearl in the deep abyss."
It is inherently free from blemish, like jade within stone; it is inherently without flaw. To those who recognize this, even thorns serve as great beams;
to those who do not recognize it, even clarified butter turns into poison.
[The Master] cited Yangshan’s question to a monk: "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Mount Lu.
Yangshan asked, "Have you ever been to the Five Elders Peak? The monk said, "I have not. Yangshan said, "Then you, Reverend, have never traveled the mountains.
Yunmen said, "This was because the ancients were compassionate; it was a discourse for descending into the weeds. The Master said: "Yunmen and Yangshan had only..."
"Your intention in accepting the jade tablet was already devoid of any intent to cede the city; you simply did not realize that the monk had already accepted it all at once.
Today, Huanglong is merely acting as a physician for a dead horse. He then took up his whisk and passed it to the monk; as the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "I am a student who has newly entered the monastic community; I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your congee?
The monk replied, "I have finished eating my congee. Zhaozhou said, "Wash your bowl and go. At that, the monk suddenly attained enlightenment.
Yunmen said, "Is there an instruction or not? If you say there is an instruction, what did he say to him? If you say..."
"If there was no instruction, how could he have attained awakening? Cuiyan said, "Master Yunmen does not know good from bad;
to speak in such a way is very much like drawing legs on a snake or growing a beard for a eunuch. Cuiyan is not like this:
if that monk had awakened in such a manner, he would have entered hell as fast as a shooting arrow. The Master said, "Although Yunmen and Cuiyan were both skilled..."
He subdues the strong and assists the weak; he abandons the wealthy to follow the poor. Yet, being unable to establish a household or found a state, he asked the monk:
"Just like the Senior Monk (Upādhyāya), you have eaten porridge this morning and washed your bowl;
are you now deluded or enlightened? The monk rose and bowed. The Master called him forward. As the monk approached, the Master said: "I have a fly-whisk; take it with you when you return."
Yunmen was once asked while on a work assignment: "I am exhausted today. If there is anyone who can explain this dialogue, please bring a question early.
He added, "If you do not ask, do not say later that the old monk deceived you. The Master then asked a monk, "Tell me—"
At that moment, what question should have been posed to avoid being deceived by Yunmen? As the monk prepared to ask, the Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
He then cited Yanguan’s instruction to the assembly: "With space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet, who can beat it? The assembly remained silent.
[The drum] was without a counterpart. Nanquan heard of this and said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have told him: 'Master Wang does not beat this broken drum.
Fayan said, "Why did Nanquan need to mention 'this broken drum'? He should simply have said, 'Master Wang does not beat it,' for it is naturally a broken drum.
The Master said, "Nanquan and Fayan only knew how to clarify what lies before them; alas!"
One cannot look back. Take, for instance, the Way of Master Yanguan: "Taking empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the drumstick—where is the place that is broken?
Can you still identify it? Even if you were able to identify it and see that place of breaking with absolute clarity, I would further ask you:
"Where is the drum itself?"
Citing Yunmen: One day, as he came out from the abbot’s quarters, a monk passed by and handed him his staff.
Yunmen took it, then handed it back to the monk. The monk was speechless. Yunmen said, "Today I have gained the advantage. The monk asked, "Why did you gain the advantage?
Yunmen replied, "I picked up my mouth to eat my rice. The Master said: "Please, Senior Monk, speak on this."
"This monk has no way to respond. Let me provide a turning phrase for him. Tell me, what kind of words should he have uttered?
The monk said, "A thing of leisure is used in times of urgency. The Master said, "I too am fortunate today. The monk asked, "Why is it that you, Master, are also fortunate?
The Master said, "I am glad to have received your response, Dharma brother."
Citing the words of Danxia: "When the hundred members have all dissolved away, one thing remains eternally numinous.
Yunmen said, "As for this staff, it cannot but be numinous. What do you call the 'hundred members'? The Master said, "They are all people who cannot save themselves."
"To call it 'one thing' is already inadequate; how much less can one speak of its being eternally efficacious?
The monk said, "Master, you too must not disparage the ancients. The Master asked, "As for your own realization, what is it like?
The monk lifted up his sitting cloth and said, "This cannot but be efficacious. The Master said, "There is gain and there is loss."

Yunmen once said, "The entire earth is medicine; the medicine is oneself. The Master then asked a monk, "Since the entire earth is medicine, why is it that it is oneself? The monk replied, "What do you call 'oneself' and 'medicine'?
The Master said, "Alas, the side-mountain is low while the main mountain is high! As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Take it!"
To know this as the talk of those who merely parrot words—

consider how when the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, saying, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. Yunmen said, "Had I seen him at that time,
I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to the dogs, so as to ensure his honor."
"Peace throughout the world. The Master asked a monk, "Tell me, does the World-Honored One have faults or not? The monk said, "He has faults.
The Master said, "Where do the faults lie? The monk said, "The fault lies in [the claim] 'I alone am honored.
The Master said, "Had I known beforehand that you would speak thus, I would not have asked at all."
[The Master] cited the case where a monk asked Yunmen: "The luminous, tranquil illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges.
Yunmen said, "Is this not the speech of the scholar Zhang Zhuo? The monk said, "It is. Yunmen said, "You have fallen into words.
The Master asked a monk, "Where do you see the point where he fell into words? The monk said, "You, Master, have fallen into words. The Master said, "Throughout the twelve hours of the day..."
"Where do you intend to establish yourself and sustain your life? The monk had no reply. The Master said, "Then come here and try to deceive me," and struck him with his whisk.
Changqing and Baofu were discussing this. A passage in the teachings states: "The Tathāgata has but one teaching; he has no second teaching.
Baofu asked, "What is the Tathāgata’s teaching? Changqing replied, "How could a deaf person hear it?
Baofu said, "I knew all along that you, elder brother, would meet people on the 'second head'. Changqing then asked Baofu, "What is the Tathāgata?"
Fokuo said, "I have not yet drunk tea after the midday meal. The Master asked a monk, "As for Changqing’s saying, 'How can a deaf person hear?
why does this fall into the second head? The monk said, "How can a deaf person hear? The Master said, "A fellow who binds himself with no rope.
Let me ask you further: 'The Tathāgata has but one teaching. How do you see that which is called 'one'?"
[The Master] said, "Principle. The monk stared at him with wide eyes. The Master said, "Up until now, you have asked one thing, yet you have answered two.
Yunmen once said: 'On level ground there are countless dead people; he who can pass through the thorn-brake forest is a true master.
The Master asked another monk, "In these times, what is commonly seen? Most are buried alive right here."
"How can you say that you have passed through the thicket of thorns? The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*) and said, "This one of mine is made of eight-foot cloth.
The Master said, "I do not believe your words."
Jiashan said, "On the tips of the hundred grasses, recognize this old monk; in the midst of the bustling marketplace, recognize the Son of Heaven.
The Master [Zhaozhou] picked up his whisk and said, "Look! The whisk has transformed into Old Jiashan coming forth.
Do you see him? A monk said, "I thank the Master for pointing it out. The Master said, "I saw that you did not look back. Now he has entered into the pillar."

Citing the Way of Hanshan: "If you wish to find a place to settle yourself, Hanshan can be preserved forever. A gentle breeze blows through the secluded pines; the closer one listens, the more exquisite the sound becomes.
Below, there is a gray-haired man muttering the teachings of Huang-Lao; for ten years he has been unable to return, having forgotten the path by which he came.
A monk asked, "What is this 'path by which one comes'? The Master pointed to the incense burner and said, "Look!"
"Hanshan is coming! Do you see him? A monk said, "What a fine incense burner. The Master said, "How embarrassing! The Master asked again, "Is that you?
Where did you just come from? The monk said, "From the quarters. The Master said, "As for one who has just come from the quarters, do they remember it now, or have they forgotten it?
The monk said, "It is simply oneself; what more is there to say about remembering?"
[The Master] forgot. The Master said, "I thought you had lost it; it turns out it was right here all along.
He cited the case of Monk Luohan, who one day entered the prefectural city with Baofu and Changqing.
The three of them saw a screen depicting peony flowers. Baofu said, "What a beautiful flower! Changqing said, "Do not let your eyes deceive you. Luohan said, "What a pity."
"A Flower. The Master said, "Based on what these three people have seen: one may be called one who transcends the Buddhas and patriarchs;
another benefits himself and is also able to benefit others; while the third not only deceives others but also deceives himself. What do you say?"
"Who is this person who deceives himself? The monk said, "Do not let your eyes deceive you.
The Master said, "From now on, go to a place that is deep in the night, quiet, and utterly devoid of people, and discuss it further with him."
To cite Nanquan: One day, seeing Deng Yinfeng approaching, he pointed to a pure pitcher and said, "The pure pitcher is an object.
There is water in the pitcher; do not touch the object, but bring me some water.
Yinfeng then took the pitcher and poured it before Nanquan, whereupon Nanquan immediately ceased speaking. Later, someone recounted this to Guizong, who said, "Deng..."
"Yin-feng was merely pouring out in disorder. The Master said, "Truly, one knows that if you walk too fast, you will not arrive;
if you walk too slowly, you will go beyond the mark. Nanquan also had a fine point of discourse, yet he was unable to bring it to full completion.
Since one can blow, one must also be able to beat time; if one cannot beat time, the blowing is in vain. Where exactly was Yin-feng’s 'pouring out in disorder'? [Examine this thoroughly]."
Examine this with the eye of study:
Take the Great Master Yunmen as an example. When he saw a monk approaching, he asked, "What have you come for? The monk replied, "I have come to request instruction.
Yunmen said, "What doubts do you have? The monk said, "I once asked the Master a question regarding a turning word, but I do not know [the answer]."
"One night's awakening is like carrying firewood; carrying firewood is one night's awakening. Yunmen struck the drum tower three times and asked, "Do you understand?
The monk said, "Everything depends on the occasion. Yunmen extended his fist and said, "I shall wrestle with you for a single bout."
"Is it so? The monk had no reply. The Master said, "It is indeed true that one can fall into a state of non-doubt.
Great Master Yunmen possessed a presence like a king, yet he fell into a pit on level ground; to this day he cannot rise.
If you wish to help him up now, I ask you, Upasaka, to provide a turning word on behalf of that monk, so that you may meet Yunmen."
"What phrase can you provide as a substitute?
He then cited the verse of the Patriarch: "Borrowing the four elements to form a body, the mind is originally unborn, arising only because of objects.
At this point, he said, "Even when one beats the grass, one must startle the snake. He then picked up his whisk and asked, "Do you see the Patriarch? The preceding object..."
"If there is no mind, then there is nothing either; sin and merit arise like illusions and likewise perish.
He then asked a monk, "What do you usually use to put on your clothes and eat your food? The monk prepared to respond, but the Master shouted him out.
Citing Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he asked Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
Bodhidharma replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? Bodhidharma replied, "I do not know.
The Master asked a monk, "Right before you is clearly Bodhidharma. How do you explain this principle of 'not knowing'? The monk said, "I do not know. The Master [said], "..."
Holding up his whisk, he said, "Dharma is here. He then cited Sanping’s verse:
"This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; There is no further sound or form to present to you. If one understands this point, there is nothing at all;
How could essence and function be divided or not? The Master said, "If they were divided, the host would be..."
This one is the host; the guest is simply the guest. If they do not separate, the host is the guest and the guest is the host. I venture to ask:
how is the matter within this resolved? "An arrow piercing the shadow of the red sun—this requires a man who shoots down the eagle."
He recited the verse on Lingyun’s awakening upon seeing peach blossoms: "For thirty years I sought the swordsman;
How many times did leaves fall and branches sprout? Since the moment I first saw the peach blossoms, To this very day, I have had no further doubt.
He then asked the monk, "Tell me, when Lingyun first saw them, were they peach blossoms or not peach blossoms? If they were peach blossoms..."
When the people of the world see these peach blossoms, they all awaken to the Way. If it were not for the peach blossoms, what would one do?
Yet here they are, presently manifest; where could you turn them away? How can you explain the principle of "seeing"? The monk was at a loss.
The Master said, "This fellow is binding himself without a rope."
He recited a verse by Maitreya: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests thousands, tens of thousands, and billions of bodies.
From time to time he appears to the people of the world, yet the people of the world do not recognize him at all. The Master said, "Why say they do not recognize him at all?
He then picked up his whisk and said, "It has always been right here! O clever fellows—if you see this, you should immediately lift it up and go!"
One day, Chongshou raised this question for a monk: "Do you see the lantern? The monk said, "I see it.
Chongshou said, "According to this one question, it is clearly seen as a single lantern;
why then does it become two? Is it because there is seeing that seeing becomes two? Or is it because there is no seeing that seeing becomes two? Can you clear up this matter?"

Even if you were able to discern it with perfect clarity, such that not even a hair’s breadth of fault remained, thirty years from now there will be another opening through which, once you have been examined, you shall be struck.
The Master Baizhang raised the case of Master Baiyun. One day, because a monk had returned from the capital, he asked him: "While you were in the capital, when you looked up—"
Seeing the vast expanse of the ocean, when one arrives here amidst a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks, you say: "Where does the sun rise?
The monk was speechless. The Master said: "In that case, even for a luminous jade disc, the examiner must be the right person;
as for a bright moon pearl, failing to recognize it only causes one to draw a sword against it. While white clouds are capable of polishing, this monk was unable to refine them."
Mó. Since he remained silent, [Mó] requested the Elder to provide a turning word on his behalf. The monk said, "He emerges from the eastern side.
The Master said, "Not only was Bāiyún defeated; even Huánglóng has been implicated."
Qianfeng rose to the hall and said: "If you raise one, you must not raise two; to let one pass is to fall into the second.
Yunmen Daoshi came forth from the assembly and said: "Yesterday, there was a man who came from Tiantai and went off to Nanyue."
Qianfeng said, "Tomorrow there will be no communal labor," and then he descended from his seat.
The Master asked a monk, "You say you have come from Tiantai; who are you? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "He is your own ancestor. Why do you not recognize him?
The monk said, "I hope the Master will give me instruction. The Master had a verse: "Qianfeng raises one, but does not raise two."
Yunmen raises his hand, adding to his spirit: "As flowers bloom and fall, let them be blown by the wind; naturally, their fragrance fills heaven and earth.

[He] cites the arrival of the Tripitaka Master Mahākarṇa from the Western Heaven at the capital, saying: "He attained the wisdom-eye that perceives the minds of others. Emperor Suzong issued an imperial decree, ordering Zhong...
The National Teacher tested him. When the Tripitaka Master saw the Teacher, he immediately prostrated and stood to the right.
The Teacher asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds? The Tripitaka Master replied, "I dare not say so. The Teacher said, "Tell me, where am I right now?
The Tripitaka Master replied, "You, O Monk, are the national teacher of this land; how could you have gone to West Sichuan to watch the boat races? The Teacher—
He asked again: "Tell me, where am I right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "The Master is the teacher of an entire nation;
how can you be here on Tianjin Bridge watching a monkey being performed? He asked a third time, using the same words as before.
After a long while, the Tripitaka Master was at a loss as to where he was. The Master rebuked him, saying: "You wild fox spirit! Your 'knowledge of others' minds' is gone!"
"Where is it? The Master had no opponent in the Tripitaka; instead, he asked the monk, "Since you claim to be a guest under the gate of Caoxi, you must surely know this matter.
Tell me, where am I, this old monk, right now? The monk was at a loss. The Master said:
"It is entirely devoid of a presiding master. The monk said, "Regarding the Tripitaka Master’s third visit, why did he not see the National Teacher?
The Master said, "If you cannot even see one now, why ask about three? If you could see one, then the three would be clear. The monk said:
"This matter cannot be attained through cultivation; only then can it be seen. The Master asked, "What do you mean by 'cultivation'? Try explaining what cultivation is.
Even if you were to cultivate it, in the end it would only lead to ruin. Cultivation and non-cultivation have no connection whatsoever.
The monk said, "If it is not attained through cultivation, then the *kalyāṇamitras* (spiritual friends) currently in the world must surely know this matter. The Master said, "You..."
Now, my questioning you lacks any authoritative basis. You need only go forth and study under various masters; simply pose your questions.
The Master is already a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); he must surely possess the wisdom-eye that perceives the minds of others.

Furthermore, tell me: where is the student right now? Observe whether he sees or does not see, and how he is guided. Then you will know for yourself whether he has arrived or not—do not deceive others.
Nonsense. One sees it directly all at once; how could it depend on the words of another?
A verse for the evening assembly.

The sun enters the hour of You (the Western Quarter). How long can this swift arrow of time last? Gathering our heads together for a mere moment, we do not realize that the weeping willows have grown upon our left elbows.
Who among us on this journey ahead has not yet returned home? For what reason do we let our ancestral legacy of a hundred years fall into neglect?
A guest asked about the meaning of the Westward Journey; I offer this as my reply:
"How many times have I been a leisurely guest in Eastern Wu? How often have I served as host in Southern Yue? It is laughable that these years have brought me to old age;
Where I may share in the dust of the world, I shall simply share in that dust."
Reading the Great Canon:

A single hair pierces through all the apertures; all the apertures are gathered within a single hair. Clouds depart from the imperial capital; waters flow back into the Yangtze and Han rivers. Reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
On a fragrant spring day, the ninetieth, Wandering bees compete to gather flowers. The fragrance returns entirely to the honeycomb; To whose house do the remaining leaves fall?

Reading the *Xinxin Ming*, even if one exhausts it to the very bottom, One still wades through wind and waves. Since antiquity, poverty has been laughable; Even a single body is regretted as too much.

An Address to the Assembly in Early Autumn: The fire-clouds of summer are about to roll away from the sky; the crescent moon gradually wanes toward its dark phase. Has the destitute son returned home yet? Together we have grown until our hair is entirely white.
There is jade within the stone, yet no one knows it; if the skilled craftsman does not come, it remains in vain. How many times I wished to speak, yet could not find the words.
Furthermore, once they have vanished like clouds and rain, they are difficult to pursue.
Since returning from Yuzhang, I have been resting at Wuweiyuan. Incidentally, I have written this:
"The whole world vies in rushing toward human affairs; amidst such busyness, I have attained a state of peaceful, high-sunbed slumber. At ease, I take one long nap in the realm of Huaxu."
A Dream: In a mere instant, soaring for several hundred years.
Because of the snow, he addresses the assembly:
"The snowy radiance falls thickly across the vast sky; whether as an omen or a blessing, do not loathe it. This is to inform those on their way who have not yet returned."
Guest: The gate of Samantabhadra has been open for a long time.
I see you escorting a monk on a journey to Mount Nanyue;
you have come to bid me farewell with your luggage packed, and you carry your flask and staff into the clouds of Xiang. The peaks of Rong are most excellent for their sounds.
Birds. In the dead of night, you likely heard them alone.

I escort Layman Hu to the edge of the pond where spring has ended and the green grass grows deep. Carrying my cane staff alone, I emerge from the cloud-covered peaks. At the third watch, by the side of the Wutong Hermitage.
Moon. Recognize this single mind before the wind. Cold moon.
Rejoicing that the mendicant has returned to the mountains, his soiled robes are temporarily hung amidst the dust.
The gates of compliance and resistance stand high and are not easily opened; the skillful response has already encompassed a thousand li.
Outside, his entire body covered in wind and snow, he rejoices in his return.
Meeting Layman Liu:
Last year we parted on the banks of Longsha; today we meet again by the shores of the Chu River. Parting and meeting—both are without [fixed nature].
The words: "Falling flowers and crying birds mark the end of spring.
Sent to the Recluse Yang:

When we spoke our parting words by the bridge of the Three Gorges, you took up your lute and returned to the west of Jade Peak. Vast and boundless are the six directions; where is the one who truly understands?
A little. Who listens to a single tune of the crows’ cries in their dreams?
The moon in the water is as clear and distinct as the moon in the sky above. Following conditions, it does not obstruct anything wherever it appears. It is a pity that one does not see it at Huating.
Guest: The cold light illuminates the night; the waves stretch empty and vast. In this quiet chamber, I observe the immediate surroundings:

the plants in the courtyard produce *zhilan* (orchids), all manifesting auspicious omens; the ground abounds with moss and lichens, all forming patterns like coins. This is simply because my single mat has no covering.
Obstructed. It is better to win the freedom to stretch out both legs and sleep.

Parting from Master Xiang in leisurely conversation, he wears the Vairocana [crown] down the green peaks; at the parting ways, speechless, he lingers but briefly. Only one wheel remains in the heavens.
The moon—ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains are still gazed upon together.

On the road during late spring, the color of the grass by the river blends with the mist into a deep green; atop the ridges, the forms of clouds drift along with the wind. Only the cuckoo, however, can speak of reality.

I ask you, O dweller in the hermitage: which of these can be relied upon?
The spring by the side of the hermitage is cold and clear, yet it has no flavor; yet it can open the heart’s knots of distress and can quench the world’s boiling turmoil.
Who would have known that these clear, shallow waters Would possess the intent to flow toward the sea?
Sent to Layman Chen Jishu:
The spring breeze blows gently; The spring days linger on. At the river bridge, there is a traveler, Returning alone to the west. There is a letter, yet it contains no words.

There is a sword concealing its brilliance, refusing to swallow the hook or bait; it blends into the mundane workings of the world. When questioned, it remains silent; when one attempts to grasp it, it is not there.
Step by step, it points toward Mount Qin, fearing that those among men who recognize it are few.
The day my former teacher entered nirvana was yesterday;
the person who departed then has not returned today. Today, as before, the person does not come; if the person does not come, they likewise do not go.
White clouds and flowing waters wander in vain. Who says the scale and ruler are level? Within the straight, there is still the crooked. Who says...
The laws of nature are uniform: sow hemp and you shall reap millet. Pity those who exhaust themselves in the pursuit of worldly fame; six times six is, after all, thirty-six.
Sent to Magistrate Yang Cigong.
In the vast silence, how many times have wind and moon risen and sunk? Sitting alone, who can speak of this mind?
Let us take up the unperforated flute of Shaolin and play a casual melody to seek out those with whom we share the same resonance.
Before the gates of the old pavilion, my thoughts have just been gathered; without a snap of the fingers, the doors are already open. Since Sudhana departed, there has been no news;
outside the gate, the spring grass remains as green as before.
Spontaneously Composed Under the Moon:

The people of today look at this moon; the people of antiquity looked at this same moon. I do not know whether it was the person of today or the person of antiquity who understood—among all those who observe the seasons—who can truly discern the timing?

When one observes the passing of time, from antiquity to the present, how many hearts have been moved by this resonance between past and present? I have always admired the Elder Nanquan for his insight.
Regarding the opportune moment: when one suddenly remembers one's hometown, one should return at once; look at him already—his departure from the mountains was late.
At the Southern Pagoda, he once realized the meaning of the *śāla* tree in years past; today, there remains only the fragrance of the *campaka*. When he departed with his single shoe, no one...
I see that the various flowers and numinous herbs are merely green.
To the question of whether one is born or unborn,
a guest comes from afar and shows me the true, true jade— never bearing the marks of carving, nor requiring the power of smelting and forging.
Vast and solitary within heaven and earth, I fear that no one may recognize me. When shall I be able to entice the impoverished son back home, causing radiance to arise within his dark chamber?
[The Master] replied: "I defer to Yan; I have seen him from afar and requested his recorded sayings."
When I was at the wall of Shaolin, I had already become a man of many words. Before the people of Luoyang have arrived, my cold sitting has already lasted for a long time.
I take up the stringless zither once more to play for you; listen as it produces the rare sound, which you shall perceive for yourself. It is neither the fragrant breeze nor flowing water;
yet it follows the flowing water down into the human world.
I have heard that when the Master entered nirvana, he came in silence and departed without a trace; coming and going are but one dream.
Fortunate is this single cypress tree by the courtyard, standing solitary through the ages and smiling at the spring breeze.
Late in the spring, I was about to depart from the prefectural city. I leave these verses to bid farewell to two or three fellow practitioners.

At the long pavilion, the smoke and willows sway in the spring breeze; the cuckoo’s cry sounds out, heralding the end of dawn and dusk. How can one bear the falling flowers that grieve the guest of Xie?

Why should one alone resent the fragrant grasses for the Prince of Wang? When we forget the trap and speak of the Way, such moments are hard to find; yet when entering the mundane world to seize the opportune moment, affairs are never at rest.
Reluctant to speak: fortunately, there are green mountains for my plan of retirement; let me cease dragging my coarse hem at the gates of nobles.
Accompanying Elder Ming on a visit to Guankxi:
the waters of Guankxi are deep and azure; who among those who arrive can fathom its depth? Flowing from antiquity to the present, it remains as clear as ever.

The Arrow. (Formerly, a monk asked Master Guankui: "I have long heard of Guankui; having arrived, I see only the hemp-soaking pond. "You see only the hemp-soaking pond, yet you do not see Guankui. "What is Guankui? [The Master replied: "As swift as a flying arrow.
Provoking the mountains and piercing through rocks like the sound of a lute, where there is a path directly ahead, how can one find room for feet?
With no gates on any four sides, how can the mind be fixed? One seeks past events but cannot find them; the yellow chrysanthemums and green bamboos merely cast their shadows in vain.
In response to the Senior Seat Xuanshou’s “Expressing Feelings While Dwelling in the Mountains”:
When the world is clear, why suffer in the dark mountain recesses? Human affairs are just like the shuttle of night-weaving. The fame and achievements of a thousand ages are but idle chatter;
this floating world of a hundred years is merely a brief passage. A profound and grave bearing can never be concealed; when one meets with the workings of Heaven, [all is resolved].

Truly lamentable! How laughable are those who wander aimlessly in pursuit of things. A flawless white jade disc—how could it ever be ground away? Gazing out from the Yiting Pavilion, I see how myriad things are so teeming and bustling.
The Peng bird and the quail each have their own aspirations; if one were to claim that each has fully realized its function, then even the straw dog would become a source of entanglement.
In the great smelting furnace, the hammer has not yet distinguished [the metal]; my wandering thoughts are in vain, lost to the spirit of *xiao-yao*.

Newly transplanted, the sunflower’s solitary root is still shallow and its growth slow; amidst the tranquil spring light, there are but one or two branches. Unchanging in its inch-sized heart, it constantly turns toward—
Day. The fragrant air returns to the time of Shanglin Park.
In summer, I sit at West Pavilion to view the peonies;
eight or nine trees cast their reflections across the pavilion. Warm breezes and rain do not fail to grace them. Do not treat this with the casual ease of mere music and song.
Scattered; when one perceives form as empty within space, it vanishes.

I have sent Huang Shusui back to discuss the return to the source; we have already refined our practice together. To maintain further "key points" would only stir up waves and storms. Before the cliff, there is naturally a sweet fragrance.
Water: Scattered as spring rain, it requires no great abundance;

gain and loss have always been decided by a single blade. Do not attempt to fix minute distinctions with the stars and constellations. Even the phoenix and peacock do not necessarily remain auspicious omens forever;
yet even the swallows and sparrows, in their flight and song, possess high value.

How could one have ceased their machinations merely for the sake of a carriage or fish? When the Way resides within the lane of Yan Hui, that is meeting with the right time. One must not forever cast aside the green mountains;
turning back one's head, the spring breeze awaits as our future appointment.
A Reply to Xie Tongyi, Pacification Commissioner of Changsha, for Inviting Me (At this time, having been requested to preside over Mount Gui, I declined his summons):
Once I took up my fishing rod upon a guest boat, For ten years I cast my line from the azure isles.
Using only the moon reflected in the water as my fragrant bait, I drew forth the golden tortoise, who mistakenly bit the hook.

Standing alone on this precarious tower, my thoughts linger with longing. My gaze reaches the end of the lake and mountains, yet my steps move slowly. Old and infirm, I am ashamed that I have returned so late;
herein it is difficult to emulate the deeds of a true man.
In response to Wang Zichun, the Privy Councillor, who has entered the Way, I present this verse:

"Clearly, clearly, clearly! Seeking spring amidst the snow, dawn within the moonlight. When weary, one leans upon the pillow with profound intent; when hungry, one eats to satiety, for the flavor is good.
Do not say that leaning and eating are merely matters of convenience. From ancient times to the present, the tracks are the same, though the paths differ. From the beginning...
Already free from all bonds, this great man pulls the tiger’s whiskers.
A verse in response to Master Jicui, sent to Chan Master Gonghui (at which time Gonghui was traveling with Du Shizhou to Changsha,
then entering Yuecheng and Mount Yue).

The spring colors of the Xiang River deepen at evening; the celestial envoy travels together with me by boat. We sail steadily upon the waters of Qu Yuan; let us refrain from ascending the city of Jia Yi.
A single cloud returns to its mountain peak; the cranes of Liaodong have departed without a trace. How far extends this vast expanse? The misty grasses stretch level with the heavens.
I show my disciples that heaven and earth are boundless, both profoundly still; do not seek to discuss this mind within them. Whether hidden or manifest, let it appear in a thousand ways;
do not pursue forms and shadows within a dream.
A Responsive Verse to Zhang, the Layman and Author of the *Exhortation to the World*.
Seeing the dust-sweeping place, dust is born anew; Recognizing the treasure, the time for its use has not yet come. How wonderful are the second and third months of Yanghe;
The flowers bloom in profusion, yet do not exhaust the spring.

If one can transform external objects, this is the Elixir of Return; picking them up with the hand as it moves, one beholds the Cavern of Heaven. There will surely be long life within the square inch of the heart-mind;
how many have reached the ultimate limit and attained the forgetting of conditions?
Above all, do not follow others in pursuit of wealth and honor; you must urgently seek to realize the treasure within yourself.
With only a few days remaining of this hundred-year span, do not say that there is another spring awaiting you on the path ahead.
Five thousand words merely point the way; following the finger, one still beholds the moon in the sky. When the moon sets and the finger is forgotten, there is no other matter;
whether sleeping drunk or sitting awake, simply follow conditions as they arise.
Reply to Layman Huang Huicheng, who has sent me his poem "Seeing the Way":

For many years you have wandered through the dust and wind upon the roads of travel; today you have returned as the old master of this house. The moon shines bright beneath the water—it is not merely night;

the lotus blooms within the fire—it has already caught the spring. Having exhausted the principles of things, you have established your household plan; meeting the timing of the era, you see the Way clearly.
Renew yourself daily. You would do well to steer your boat across the surging waves; do not let your coming and going be stalled at the lost ford.

As the sun sets on excursions through the countryside, day after day, a hundred years pass in vain emergence and submergence. Amidst this vast expanse of dust and soil, how few recognize the true nest?
I have always admired Yunmen’s noble character: he did not reveal his secret mechanisms, so people could not recognize him. Deep and vast, the pure wind departed and did not return;
on the road to Huangmei, thorns and brambles gradually grew.
A Harmonious Response to Official Lin’s “Ode on Illuminating the Way,” Sent to Me:
Seeing delusion, I seek the true medicine; The true medicine cures the delusion. When both medicine and disease are forgotten, How can the perceived realm ever be a realm?
It is not that the whole body is non-existent; it is that the whole body is existent. One must recognize this mind of right and wrong, which has already existed prior to heaven and earth.
One seeks to rest, yet finds no rest; one seeks to understand, yet finds no understanding. The moon of the mind is naturally solitary and full; heaven and earth are all illuminated by it as one.
Existence and non-existence are fundamentally not two; to hold them as two is to fall into error. If you cling to a "non-dual" mind, you darken the mirror of original nature.
When the winds of the river of craving are fierce, the waves are coarse; when the sun of wisdom shines, the waves wither of their own accord.
There is no need to hoist sails or ply oars; in the end, no effort at all is required.
In sending off Yu Hongfan, the Judicial Commissioner:

Who says the swan and crane are lofty? They naturally possess wings that touch the clouds. Who says the swallow and sparrow are lowly? They naturally possess the ambition of the *péng* and *hāo* trees.

How carefree are these two creatures! Both flying and singing, they each find their place. Once a man perceives the heart of Heaven and Earth, for him mist to rise and clouds to drift is likewise easy.
Two verses in response to Huang Shusui.
Do not laboriously ask for the ferry crossing at the riverhead; the news from the riverhead is already painfully explained.
Old Lu crossed the pass with nothing else to do, yet he vainly used his robe and bowl to deceive later generations.
Summer clouds rise as wondrous peaks; cold springs pour forth like flying silken ribbons. Every thing possesses its own function; herein there is no change. Have you not seen?
The wind does not wait for the moon to be cold; fire does not wait for the sun to be hot. And have you not seen?
The form within a mirror, the flowers in the void—when one gazes upon them, they are truly marvelous and sublime.
I bid farewell to Master Chongliang, who once forged and refined [the Way] beneath Mount Zhurong. Amidst the common throng, none could distinguish the true from the false.
When the winds and clouds gather at Vulture Peak, there will surely be those who recognize the true sound.

Seeing off Wu De-fu, the Judicial Official, at Haimen Mountain—where the paths are perilous and tracks cut off. Having severed the sturdy barrier, his faith is now unimpeded. The foundation for an era of Great Peace exists within himself;
it matters not whether one is north, south, east, or west.
To find fire within water is rare in this world; watching it makes one’s doubts all the more peculiar. Since ancient times, there have been no masters or disciples;
yet now, the old barbarian is permitted to know.
Fundamentally there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, though many paths appear; the pupils within the eyes are not easily seen.
Only fearing that they cannot be retained therein, they fall again as drenching rain upon the world.
Seeing Master Zhang off, he observes that the springtime peach blossoms are at their finest; again, he waves his whip and departs through the mountain gate.
Before the wind, this single note is impossible to conceal—it has already revealed Lingyun’s supreme mechanism.
In response to Zhang Chuci, two verses:

From of old, there have been illnesses and their remedies; The arising of delusion is likewise caused by the claim that "the True exists. If delusional illness is forgotten, the true remedy is exhausted;
All is transparently clear—the person of former times.

If one clings to clarity and brightness, it turns instead into an affliction; only when the myriad dharmas are interpenetrating is there truth. Curves and straightness, squares and circles do not intersect;
with what dharma could one intend to entrust oneself to whom?
In response to the "Song of Shaolin" sent by Mr.
Zou of Xinwu: Truly difficult to repay with a song in return. Old and infirm, how can I hope to continue his legacy? Fortunately, I am entrusted to the green mountains like a hidden leopard;
I regret that I lack the "surplus blade" to dissect the whole ox. My lifelong pursuits have long been neglected; My fame through the ages is but a source of laughter.
I have retired; yet the wind and moon of my old garden remain. For your sake, I preserve them for your travels within this community.

Retiring from office, I attend to daily affairs, no longer dwelling in the temples of the Tang dynasty; now idly a monk in the land of Song. My livelihood consists of three robes of patchwork and an old companion, a single staff of rattan.

Seeking alms, I go as circumstances lead; encountering mountains, I ascend them at will. Should we meet, do not laugh at one another; this is not merely the capability of those from Lingnan. Dwelling in my hermitage, I am moved by these reflections:
with a bamboo staff, a palm-leaf hat, and robes of *bìluó* vines, I have entered deep into Longfeng Peak and closed my door alone. I rejoice in the sweet serenity of these woods and springs.
In nature, fish and birds alike forget their artifice; in vain do we polish our spiritual practices through the ages. Cease seeking right and wrong within the city of *gandharva-nagara*;
why prattle on with strange words about Huang-Lao? Could you not join hands and return home together in the same carriage?
Sending Zen Practitioner Ben back to the capital to travel through the monasteries, his Way shines ever more brightly. Packing his robes to return home, how long-lasting is his inspiration!
Since white clouds are, after all, mindless things, they too follow the western wind back to the imperial city.
Written on the Wall of the Layman Zhou: I see many people who do not speak; I conceal my breath to pass the remainder of my life. I have a house roofed with thatch and bamboo; no one knows my name.

The solitary lamp and the silence of the forest sounds; the cold moon and the clarity of the stone pond. It is not that I cherish lofty principles; the Kun and Peng birds simply have their own course.
Master Yan composed a verse to bid him farewell. I hastily penned this to see him off:
The frost wind blows piercingly; frost leaves fly everywhere. Upon the long and short pavilions, a traveler returns south. His remaining writings are like bird tracks in the mist.

Tattered robes are covered in dust; the perilous cliff rises ten thousand fathoms high. With a single lean bamboo staff, I am like a wild goose soaring to distant heights, leaving only those who hunt with arrows to wonder at my presence.
As I step out the gate for ten thousand miles, who will bid me farewell? Not even an inch of grass grows here—this I know only within myself.
Whenever the Master was in his room, he would show his fist to people and say: "If you see it as a fist, that is contact;
if you do not see it as a fist, that is avoidance. How do you, Venerable Elder, see it? When a monk asked this question, the Master answered him with this.
Huanglong has a fist. Whether one attains the skin or the marrow, he presents it directly and clearly;
yet this is already like mixing mud with water.
Huanglong has a fist. When raised, there is no other principle: one must break through the secure barrier; all are thus.
As for one's own practice:
Huanglong has a fist. Whether it be noble or base, let you set the price as you wish. Yet if you step forward intending to deliberate upon it, you will instead become the talk of the age.
Postscript to the Recorded Sayings of Huanglong Anzhu,
composed by Wang Shao of Fuyang.
Fuyangzi said: "I have often exhorted students that in studying the Way of the Sages, they should all seek it beyond mere words, phrases, and commentaries.
As for the Way of Heaven and the principles of Yin and Yang, these must be sought even beyond calculations and calendrical systems."

Now that I have met Master Huanglong Xin and he has revealed the ultimate Way to me, it becomes clear that what is called the principle of the sage’s nature and life lies beyond all lifelong study and intellectual thought.
Alas! As the ancients said, "The Buddha-dharma is transmitted entirely through the mind. Is this not so?
How empty it is! Nevertheless, even if one wishes to transmit its mind, it cannot be attained; thus, that which is called "attainment" has never been attained.
Let students reflect upon this. Preface written on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Yuanfeng era.
